days.description: Today we are learning Introduction to Python.
days.title: Introduction to Python

topics.theoryContent:
A computer only understands very simple instructions. To make it do useful work — calculate a salary, check stock in a warehouse, or send an email — someone has to write down the steps. A programming language is simply a way to write those steps clearly enough for the machine to carry them out.

Python is one such language, and it is special because it reads almost like plain English. Where other languages force you to write a lot of punctuation, Python lets you focus on the logic: "if the customer is a VIP, give a discount".

Think of Python as the assistant who takes your written instructions and converts them into machine action. You write WHAT you want; Python handles the tedious translation.

It was created by Guido van Rossum in 1991 and has grown into one of the most widely used languages in the world.
topics.title: What is Python?

topics.theoryContent:
READABLE — Python's design deliberately keeps code close to everyday language. Teams can read each other's code and understand it faster, which makes real projects cheaper to maintain.

LARGE ECOSYSTEM — thousands of ready-made libraries exist for nearly every job: requests for web calls, pandas for tables of data, numpy for mathematics. A library is code someone else already wrote, so you reuse it instead of rebuilding it.

WIDE APPLICATION — the same language works for websites, automation scripts, data analysis, artificial intelligence, and backend systems. Companies prefer it because one language covers many problems.

BEGINNER FRIENDLY — the simple syntax means a first program is a few lines, not a book of boilerplate. New programmers see results quickly and keep their motivation.

STRONG COMMUNITY — millions of developers, free tutorials, and long-standing answers on every error you will meet. When you are stuck, the solution is almost always one search away.

PRODUCTIVE — because you write less code for the same result, features ship faster. (One honest note: Python is not always the fastest language to EXECUTE. It is popular because it is fast to WRITE — and for most business logic, that matters more.)
topics.title: Why Python is popular

topics.theoryContent:
WEB DEVELOPMENT — platforms like Instagram and Spotify use Python on their servers to handle millions of users. Frameworks like Django and Flask power the logic behind websites.

AUTOMATION — anything repetitive can be scripted: renaming 500 files, reading every email attachment, backing up folders, generating daily reports. Offices run these scripts overnight.

DATA ANALYSIS — spreadsheets that grow too large are moved into pandas, where trends, averages and clean tables can be computed in seconds.

ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND MACHINE LEARNING — most AI models, from recommendation engines to language models, are trained using Python frameworks like TensorFlow and PyTorch.

SCIENTIFIC COMPUTING — researchers in physics, biology and finance use Python for calculations and visualisation.

SCRIPTING — short utility programs that glue systems together: extract data from one system, transform it, and load it into another.

You will practice all of these directions in this course. Today you only need the first step: getting Python running on your machine.
topics.title: Python applications

topics.theoryContent:
PYTHON DEVELOPER — builds and maintains software where Python is the primary language. Comfortable with libraries, testing and deployment.

BACKEND DEVELOPER — builds the server side of applications: APIs, databases, business logic. Python is one of the most common backend languages in job listings.

DATA ANALYST — works with tables of business data, cleans them, and produces reports and dashboards. Tools: pandas, spreadsheets, SQL.

DATA SCIENTIST — goes deeper: builds models that predict behaviour, finds patterns, and presents conclusions to non-technical teams.

MACHINE LEARNING ENGINEER — turns data science prototypes into production systems that run at scale, using frameworks and cloud infrastructure.

AI ENGINEER — builds products that use AI, such as chatbots, recommendation systems and computer vision.

AUTOMATION ENGINEER — designs scripts and tools that remove manual work from business processes.

The exact title does not matter today. Every one of these roles begins with the same fundamentals you will learn in this course: variables, conditions, loops, functions and data structures.
topics.title: Python career paths

topics.theoryContent:
You need two things on your computer: the Python software itself, and a way to write and run programs.

1. Go to python.org/downloads and click the download button for your operating system.
2. Run the installer. IMPORTANT: tick the box that says "Add Python to PATH". If you skip this, the python command may not work in the terminal.
3. Finish the install.

To confirm it worked, open a terminal (Command Prompt on Windows) and type:

python --version

You should see something like "Python 3.12.x". If you see a version number, Python is installed correctly.
topics.title: Installing Python

topics.theoryContent:
Python alone gives you a command line, but writing real programs is much easier with a proper editor. VS Code is a free editor made by Microsoft that is the industry default for Python beginners and professionals alike.

Why VS Code is useful for Python:
- Colours the code so mistakes stand out (syntax highlighting).
- Shows hints as you type (IntelliSense).
- Runs your program with one click.
- Built-in terminal, so you never have to leave the editor.

Steps:
1. Go to code.visualstudio.com and download VS Code.
2. Install it with the default options.
3. Open VS Code, go to the Extensions panel (the puzzle-piece icon) and install the "Python" extension published by Microsoft.

You now have an editor that understands Python. Installing VS Code is a tooling step, not a programming concept — but it saves you hours of frustration later.
topics.title: Installing VS Code

topics.theoryContent:
Python is an INTERPRETED language. That means a program called the interpreter reads your Python code line by line and carries out each instruction immediately. It is like a live translator at a meeting: you speak a sentence, the translator passes it on, then you speak the next.

This is different from COMPILED languages like C, where the entire program is translated to machine code before it can run at all.

The practical consequence: you can run a single line and see the result instantly. That makes Python perfect for experimentation. Type a line, see the output, adjust, try again.

The flow is always the same:
You write code in a file  →  the interpreter reads it  →  it performs the actions  →  output is displayed.

A mental model: the interpreter is the "brain" that turns your instructions into computer actions. When your code has a mistake, the interpreter stops and tells you where.
topics.title: The Python interpreter

topics.theoryContent:
There are three basic ways to run Python. Learn all three today because you will use each one at different times.

1. THE INTERACTIVE INTERPRETER — type "python" in a terminal and you get a prompt (>>>). Every line you type runs immediately. Great for quick experiments.

2. RUNNING A FILE — write code in a .py file, then in the terminal run:
python myprogram.py
The whole file executes from top to bottom. This is how real programs are run.

3. VS CODE — open your .py file, then click the play button (top-right) or press Ctrl+F5. VS Code runs the file and shows the output in the terminal panel below. Most of this course will use this method.

A note on naming: never name a file python.py — it can confuse the interpreter. Use meaningful names like hello.py or report.py.
topics.title: Running Python programs

topics.theoryContent:
The print() function is how a program shows information to the user. Whatever you put inside the brackets gets displayed on the screen.

The classic first example is:

print("Hello World")

It demonstrates the syntax, but it does not show WHY print() matters. Real programs use print() to communicate status: a support desk showing a customer's current state, a delivery system confirming a package is out for delivery, a billing system printing an amount due.

Consider a delivery company. It needs to display a customer's order status. Using print(), the program produces meaningful output:

Customer:
Ravi

Order:
Laptop Stand

Quantity:
2

Status:
Out for Delivery

Every line of that output is produced by one print() statement. print() is how your program talks to the person using it. The syntax is simple:
- print( )  — the word print followed by brackets.
- " "       — double quotes (or single quotes) around text that should be shown as-is. Text inside quotes is called a string.
- ,         — commas separate multiple pieces, separated by spaces in the output.
topics.title: print() — producing output

topics.theoryContent:
A comment is a note you leave in the code for humans. The interpreter completely ignores it — it exists only to explain, remind, or warn the next person who reads the code (which is often you, months later).

In Python, a single-line comment starts with the # symbol and runs to the end of the line:

# This line explains what the code below does
print("Status: Out for Delivery")

When comments help:
- Explaining WHY a choice was made ("# lower the price only after 60 days, per policy").
- Documenting a non-obvious formula or a business rule.
- Marking a section of a long file.
- Temporarily disabling a line while you test (comment it out).

Avoiding unnecessary comments:
- Do not repeat what the code obviously says. Writing "# print the status" above print("Status: Out for Delivery") adds noise.
- The code already tells you WHAT. Comments should tell you WHY, or the important detail that is not visible.

The habit of writing brief, honest comments is one of the most underrated skills in programming. Teams judge code by how quickly a newcomer can understand it — comments are the shortcut.
topics.title: Comments

days.description: Today we are learning Variables, Keywords, and Data Types.
days.title: Variables, Keywords, and Data Types

codeExamples.code:
customer = "Ravi"
order_item = "Laptop Stand"
quantity = 2
print(customer)
print(order_item)
print(quantity)
codeExamples.explanation: Each value is stored under a name, then print() reads the box and displays what is inside.
codeExamples.title: Storing and using a variable

codeExamples.code:
balance = 1499.50
print("Old balance:", balance)
balance = 1750.00
print("New balance:", balance)
codeExamples.explanation: The second assignment replaces the value in the box. The print statements show the value that was in the box at that moment.
codeExamples.title: Updating a variable

topics.theoryContent:
A variable is a named box in which a program stores a value. Instead of typing a number or a name every time you need it, you store it once under a name and use the name from then on.

name = "Ravi"
age = 21
balance = 1499.50

The = sign is called assignment. It does not mean "is equal to"; it means "store the value on the right into the name on the left". Read it as "name gets Ravi".

A variable can be updated anytime — that is why it is called a VARIABLE. Later in the program you can change it:

balance = 1499.50
balance = 1750.00   # now it holds the new value

Real systems do this constantly: a shopping cart total grows as items are added, a game score changes, a temperature reading is refreshed each minute.
topics.title: Variables

topics.theoryContent:
Python is strict about what names you are allowed to use:
- Names may contain letters, digits and underscores.
- A name must NOT start with a digit. 1st_name is invalid; first_name is fine.
- No spaces are allowed — use underscores instead: customer_name, not customer name.
- Names are case-sensitive: total and Total are two different variables.
- You cannot use Python keywords (see the next topic).

Beyond the rules, good naming is a professional habit:
- Use descriptive names: total_marks instead of t or x.
- Use lowercase with underscores between words (snake_case): student_email.
- Never name a variable print or input — it will hide the built-in function.

Bad name: m = 1499.50
Good name: monthly_fee = 1499.50

Readable names turn a confusing script into a document.
topics.title: Variable naming rules

topics.theoryContent:
Keywords are words that Python has reserved for its own grammar. They have a fixed meaning and CANNOT be used as variable names. Trying to use one gives a SyntaxError.

Some keywords you will meet soon: if, else, for, while, def, return, import, class, not, and, or, in, is, True, False, None.

if = 5   # ERROR — if is a keyword

You do not need to memorise the full list now. The rule to remember: if your variable name triggers an error in a different colour and the name is a plain English word like if or for, it is probably a keyword — rename it.

You can see the full list at any time by running:

import keyword
print(keyword.kwlist)
topics.title: Keywords

topics.theoryContent:
In many languages you must declare the type of a variable before using it ("this box will hold a whole number"). Python does not: you just assign a value, and Python figures out the type automatically.

data = 5        # Python knows this is a whole number
data = "hello"  # now the same name holds text — Python allows it

This is called DYNAMIC typing: the type is decided at the moment of assignment and can change later.

The freedom is convenient, but it puts a responsibility on you: keep a name's meaning consistent. Changing the same name from a number to text mid-program is a classic source of confusing bugs. Use one name for one kind of thing.

For today, the takeaway is: you write the value, Python infers the type.
topics.title: Dynamic typing

topics.theoryContent:
int (short for integer) holds whole numbers — positive, negative or zero, with no decimal point.

quantity = 2
year = 2026
score = -10

int values are used for counting things: seats on a bus, items in a cart, pages in a document. Because they represent exact counts, arithmetic on them is exact.

Whole-number division is a common early surprise: 7 // 2 gives 3 (the remainder is dropped). The // operator is integer division, and % gives the remainder: 7 % 2 gives 1.
topics.title: The int type (whole numbers)

topics.theoryContent:
float holds numbers with a decimal point — measurements, prices, percentages.

price = 1499.50
height = 5.9
average = 74.25

Use floats whenever the real-world value is not a whole count: money, weight, temperature, time in minutes.

One honest caveat: floats are stored in binary, so some decimals are approximate (0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004). For ordinary display that is invisible. For financial totals you would later use the Decimal module. Do not worry about it today — just know the difference between a count (int) and a measurement (float).
topics.title: The float type (decimals)

codeExamples.code:
first = "Ravi"
last = "Reddy"
full = first + " " + last
print(full)
codeExamples.explanation: The + operator joins strings. The middle string adds the space between the two names.
codeExamples.title: Combining strings

topics.theoryContent:
str (string) holds text: names, addresses, status messages, labels. A string is written between quotes.

name = "Anita"
message = "Out for Delivery"
empty = ""

You can use single quotes or double quotes, as long as you are consistent within a string. Strings join with + and repeat with *:

first = "Ravi"
last = "Reddy"
print(first + " " + last)   # Ravi Reddy
print("beep" * 3)           # beepbeepbeep

Real systems store nearly every human-readable piece of information as a string: customer names, emails, order numbers, city names.
topics.title: The str type (text)

topics.theoryContent:
bool holds only two values: True or False. Booleans are the answer to yes/no questions a program asks: is the account active? is stock available? is the customer a VIP?

is_active = True
has_stock = False

Booleans will become powerful tomorrow and on Day 5 when the program makes decisions:

if is_active:
    print("Welcome back")

For now, learn to create them (True/False with a capital first letter — true and false are not valid Python) and to read them as yes/no answers.
topics.title: The bool type (True / False)

topics.theoryContent:
None represents the absence of a value — a box that exists but is empty. It is Python's way of saying "no value here yet".

phone = None      # we do not know this customer's phone number yet

None is useful when a value is not known or not applicable: an optional field in a form, a result that has not been computed yet.

Two things to remember:
- None is not the number 0 and not an empty string. It is its own special value meaning "nothing".
- When a program is "ready" to compare values against None (much later), the correct check uses the is keyword: phone is None.

None prints as the word None.
topics.title: The None type (nothing)

codeExamples.code:
print(type(10))
print(type(10.5))
print(type("Python"))
print(type(False))
print(type(None))
codeExamples.explanation: Each line prints the class of the value. Notice that a number without a decimal point is int, with a decimal point is float.
codeExamples.title: Inspecting the type of each value

topics.theoryContent:
type() tells you the type of a value. Pass the value (or the variable holding it) and it returns the type:

print(type(5))        # <class 'int'>
print(type(5.0))      # <class 'float'>
print(type("hi"))     # <class 'str'>
print(type(True))     # <class 'bool'>
print(type(None))     # <class 'NoneType'>

This is a debugging tool as much as a learning tool. When a program misbehaves, the first question is often "what type is this actually?" type() answers it instantly.
topics.title: type() — asking what kind of value it is

topics.theoryContent:
Every value lives at a location in the computer's memory. id() returns a number that identifies that location while the value exists.

name = "Ravi"
print(id(name))    # e.g. 140712345678912

In real work you will rarely call id() directly. What matters is the idea it demonstrates: variables are names that point to boxes in memory, and two different variables CAN point to the same box.

Later, when you study lists and objects, id() becomes the honest proof of whether two names really share the same data or hold separate copies. For today, just run it once to see that every value has an address.
topics.title: id() — the memory address of a value

Convert between types with int(), float(), str(), bool()

This exact flow — read, convert, calculate, display — is the skeleton of every interactive calculator-style program.

days.description: Today we are learning Input and Type Conversion.
days.title: Input and Type Conversion

codeExamples.code:
name = input("Enter your name: ")
print("Hello,", name)
codeExamples.explanation: The program stops and waits until the user types a name and presses Enter, then greets them.
codeExamples.title: A name greeting

codeExamples.code:
phone = input("Enter your phone number: ")
print("We will contact you at", phone)
codeExamples.explanation: Phone numbers are stored as text because they are labels, not values to calculate with.
codeExamples.title: Reading a phone number

topics.theoryContent:
A program that always prints the same thing is a recording. A real program reacts to the person using it. input() pauses the program, shows a prompt, waits for the user to type something, and hands that text back to your program.

name = input("Enter your name: ")
print("Hello,", name)

The text inside the brackets is the prompt shown to the user. Whatever the user types is stored in the variable.

An important detail: the user's answer always comes back as a STRING. Even if the person types a number, you receive text like "21" — not the number 21. Converting it is the next topic.
topics.title: input() — getting information from the user

topics.theoryContent:
When a user types "21", the terminal only knows it received the characters 2 and 1. Python therefore hands you the string "21". If your program then tries to do arithmetic, it fails:

age = input("Age: ")
print(age + 1)   # TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

"21" + 1 makes no sense to Python — adding text and a number is undefined. The fix is to CONVERT the text into a number before using it as one.

This single misunderstanding causes a large share of beginner errors. Remember the rule: input comes in as text; numbers must be converted before arithmetic.
topics.title: Why input() always returns a string

codeExamples.code:
age = int(input("Enter your age: "))
print("Next year you will be", age + 1)
codeExamples.explanation: The string from input() is converted with int() and only then used in arithmetic.
codeExamples.title: Reading and using a number

topics.theoryContent:
int() takes text (or another number) and converts it to a whole number.

int("21")      # 21
int(3.9)       # 3   (the decimal part is truncated, not rounded)

If the text is not a number, conversion fails:

int("abc")     # ValueError: invalid literal for int()

The classic pattern for reading a number from the user:

age = int(input("Enter your age: "))
print("Next year you will be", age + 1)

Here input() returns "21", int() converts it to 21, and now arithmetic works.

Note what int(3.9) does: it drops the decimal part toward zero. Use it when the real-world value must be a whole count.
topics.title: int() — converting to a whole number

codeExamples.code:
weight = float(input("Enter weight in kg: "))
print("Weight in grams:", weight * 1000)
codeExamples.explanation: The string is converted to a float so that multiplication works.
codeExamples.title: Converting a measurement

topics.theoryContent:
float() converts text or a number into a decimal (float) value — for measurements and prices.

float("74.5")    # 74.5
float("10")      # 10.0
float("7.5cm")   # ValueError — extra characters are not allowed

Reading a measurement:

weight = float(input("Enter weight in kg: "))
print("Weight in grams:", weight * 1000)

The same rule as int(): the text must look like a number, otherwise you get a ValueError.
topics.title: float() — converting to a decimal number

codeExamples.code:
quantity = 2
print("You ordered " + str(quantity) + " items.")
codeExamples.explanation: Without str(), Python would try to add text and a number and raise an error.
codeExamples.title: Joining a number into a sentence

topics.theoryContent:
str() converts any value into its text form.

str(25)          # "25"
str(1499.50)     # "1499.5"
str(True)        # "True"

Why would you convert a number to text? When you want to join it into a longer message. Numbers cannot be added to strings with +, so you convert first:

qty = 2
message = "Items ordered: " + str(qty)
print(message)

str() is also used automatically when a number is printed next to text with a comma — print("Total:", total) works without str() because print() converts internally.
topics.title: str() — converting to text

topics.theoryContent:
bool() converts any value to True or False, following one rule: almost everything is True, and only a few "empty" values are False.

bool(0)        # False
bool(1)        # True
bool("")       # False  (empty string)
bool("text")   # True
bool(None)     # False

This matters for programs written later when conditions decide between two paths. The practical rule for today: 0, empty text, None and False all convert to False; everything else converts to True.

You will rarely call bool() directly — you will use values in conditions and let Python judge them. But knowing the rule explains many "why is it showing the wrong branch?" moments.
topics.title: bool() — converting to a boolean

topics.theoryContent:
Implicit conversion happens automatically when Python joins values of different types without being asked. The most common case is int meeting float:

5 + 2.5        # 7.5  — the int 5 is silently upgraded to 5.0

Python widens the int to a float so the calculation can proceed exactly. You can see it with type():

print(type(5 + 2.5))   # <class 'float'>

Notice what does NOT happen implicitly: str and numbers are never merged automatically. "5" + 5 is an error, and "5" * 5 repeats the string five times instead of multiplying.

Implicit conversion is convenient and usually invisible. It becomes important when you divide: 7 / 2 gives 3.5 (a float) even though both operands are ints — Python converts to float so the answer is exact.
topics.title: Implicit conversion

codeExamples.code:
price = float(input("Enter price per item: "))
quantity = int(input("Enter quantity: "))
total = price * quantity
print("Total bill:", total)
codeExamples.explanation: Both inputs are converted to numbers as soon as they arrive, then the arithmetic works on real numbers.
codeExamples.title: Complete input + conversion flow

topics.theoryContent:
Explicit conversion is when YOU call int(), float(), str() or bool() deliberately. You are telling Python: "take this value and turn it into this type."

They are used at the boundary where real-world data enters the program:
- input() gives strings → convert to numbers with int()/float().
- A number must be placed inside a message → convert with str().
- A calculation must produce a whole count → int().

The general advice: convert once, as early as possible. Read the input, convert it, store the converted value in a clearly named variable, and do all further work with the number.

A typical flow:
- ask for the price (string)
- convert to float
- ask for the quantity (string)
- convert to int
- compute total = price * quantity
- display with print()
topics.title: Explicit conversion

commonMistakes: Writing = when you mean == — one of the most common errors of all time.
Forgetting that / always returns a float, even for 10 / 2 (5.0).
Expecting 7 / 2 to be 3 instead of 3.5.
Writing and/or in a condition but putting brackets in the wrong place, so the meaning changes.
Comparing a value to None with == instead of is.
Assuming bitwise operators are the same as logical ones: & is not the same as and.

codeExamples.code:
minutes = 100
full_sessions = minutes // 30
leftover = minutes % 30
print("Full sessions:", full_sessions)
print("Leftover minutes:", leftover)
codeExamples.explanation: Floor division finds whole sessions; modulo finds the remainder — together they break a quantity into groups and leftovers.
codeExamples.title: Calculating with mixed operators

topics.theoryContent:
Arithmetic operators do the maths:
+  addition         5 + 2 = 7
-  subtraction      5 - 2 = 3
*  multiplication   5 * 2 = 10
/  division         5 / 2 = 2.5  (always gives a float)
// floor division   5 // 2 = 2   (whole part only)
%  modulo           5 % 2 = 1    (the remainder)
** power            5 ** 2 = 25

The ones beginners find new are //, % and **. Floor division answers "how many whole times fits?" and modulo answers "what is left over?"

Examples from real life:
- 100 // 30 = 3 → three 30-minute sessions fit into 100 minutes.
- 100 % 30 = 10 → ten minutes are left after those sessions.
- 2 ** 10 = 1024 → the number of ways ten switches can be on/off.

Division always produces a float in Python, even when it divides evenly: 10 / 2 is 5.0.
topics.title: Arithmetic operators

codeExamples.code:
total = 0
total += 120   # first customer
total += 45    # second customer
total += 80    # third customer
print("Total collected:", total)
codeExamples.explanation: Each += adds to the running total. The pattern is exactly how a cash register accumulates sales across the day.
codeExamples.title: A running total at a stall

topics.theoryContent:
Assignment operators are shortcuts for "update this variable using its current value".

x = 10
x += 5    # same as x = x + 5   → x is now 15
x -= 3    # same as x = x - 3   → x is now 12
x *= 2    # same as x = x * 2   → x is now 24
x /= 4    # same as x = x / 4   → x is now 6.0
x %= 4    # same as x = x % 4   → x is now 2.0
x //= 2   # floor-divide and assign
x **= 2   # square and assign

They exist because "update the counter" is such a common operation — a running total, a score, a queue position — and writing it twice is wasteful and error-prone.

The meaning is always the same: take the current value, apply the operation with the right-hand value, store the result back.
topics.title: Assignment operators

codeExamples.code:
marks = 74
print(marks >= 70)
print(marks == 100)
print(marks != 0)
codeExamples.explanation: Each comparison evaluates to a True or False value that a later condition can use.
codeExamples.title: Comparison producing booleans

topics.theoryContent:
Comparison operators ask a question about two values and answer True or False:
==  equal         5 == 5 is True,  5 == 6 is False
!=  not equal     5 != 6 is True
>   greater than  6 > 5 is True
<   less than     5 < 6 is True
>=  greater or equal
<=  less or equal

The two-character == is easy to confuse with the single = assignment. Remember: = stores a value, == asks a question.

Comparisons return a bool, which is exactly what the conditions on Day 5 will need.

score = 74
print(score >= 70)   # True — eligible for the certificate threshold
print(score >= 80)   # False
topics.title: Comparison operators

codeExamples.code:
credit_score = 720
income = 30000
approved = (credit_score >= 700) and (income > 25000)
print("Loan approved:", approved)
codeExamples.explanation: Both conditions must be true for and to return True. Change either number and the result changes.
codeExamples.title: Combining conditions for a loan

topics.theoryContent:
Logical operators combine True/False values:
and  — True only when both sides are True
or   — True when at least one side is True
not  — flips True to False and False to True

Examples from a loan desk:
- approve if credit_score >= 700 AND income > 25000
- send offer if customer is_vip OR first_time_buyer
- block if NOT customer_active

Python evaluates and/or lazily (left to right, stopping as soon as the answer is known). Use brackets to make complex conditions readable:

eligible = (age >= 18) and (has_id)
topics.title: Logical operators

topics.theoryContent:
is checks whether two names point to the SAME object in memory — not whether their values are equal. For values that are never duplicated (like True, False, None) is and == behave the same. For values that can exist as separate copies, they differ.

For today, the one rule worth keeping: check None with is, not ==.

phone = None
print(phone is None)     # True — the standard way
print(phone == None)     # works, but is is the accepted style

Why have both? == compares the contents, is compares the identity (which box in memory). Two separate variables can hold equal contents but be different objects. You will see the distinction matter on Day 14 when lists are studied — two lists can have identical items yet be two different objects.
topics.title: Identity operators (is / is not)

codeExamples.code:
item = "laptop"
stock = ["laptop", "mouse", "keyboard"]
print("Item available:", item in stock)
codeExamples.explanation: in searches the list and returns True when the exact item is present.
codeExamples.title: Checking if an item is in stock

topics.theoryContent:
in asks whether a value appears inside a collection — a string, list or tuple.

"ravi" in "hello ravi"       # True
"x" in "python"              # False
"laptop" in ["laptop", "mouse", "keyboard"]   # True
"pen" not in ["laptop", "mouse"]              # True

For strings, in checks whether the text appears as a substring (a piece of the text). For lists, it checks whether an item is present.

Real use: validating a selection.

choice = input("Select a plan: ")
if choice in ["basic", "pro", "enterprise"]:
    print("Valid plan")
topics.title: Membership operators (in / not in)

topics.theoryContent:
Bitwise operators work on the individual binary bits of integers. Most business code never uses them, but they appear in performance-sensitive or systems-level code, so you should recognise them:
&  bitwise AND       5 & 3  →  1
|  bitwise OR        5 | 3  →  7
^  bitwise XOR       5 ^ 3  →  6
~  bitwise NOT       ~5     →  -6
<< left shift        1 << 4 →  16
>> right shift       16 >> 2 → 4

They treat numbers as binary. For example 5 is binary 101 and 3 is binary 011; AND keeps only bits set in both: 001 = 1.

When are they used in practice? Permissions flags (a single number packing several on/off settings), graphics work, and hardware/embedded code. A beginner project will almost never need them — but they belong to the operator toolbox and to the syllabus. Understand the idea now; reach for them only when the job truly calls for bit-level work.
topics.title: Bitwise operators

codeExamples.code:
price = 100
qty = 3
discount = 50
total = (price * qty) - discount
print("Bill after discount:", total)
codeExamples.explanation: Brackets make it obvious that the multiplication happens first, then the discount is subtracted.
codeExamples.title: Precedence in a real calculation

topics.theoryContent:
When several operators appear in one expression, Python applies them in a fixed order — the same precedence mathematics teaches:

1. brackets ( )
2. **  (power)
3. *  /  //  %  (multiply, divide, floor, modulo)
4. +  -  (add, subtract)
5. comparisons  ==  !=  <  >  <=  >=
6. not  and  or  (logical, in that order)

So 2 + 3 * 4 is 14 (multiplication first), and (2 + 3) * 4 is 20.

Two rules to live by:
- When in doubt, use brackets. They cost nothing and remove all ambiguity for the reader.
- Never rely on remembering that and binds tighter than or — put brackets around the parts you mean.

price * qty + tax  →  (price * qty) + tax  — clearer, same result.
topics.title: Operator precedence

Writing else with a condition: else (x > 5): is invalid — use elif.

days.title: Conditional Statements

topics.theoryContent:
A boolean expression is any piece of code that evaluates to True or False. You built them on Day 4: comparisons and logical combinations.

age >= 18
score >= 70 and score <= 100
status == "approved"

Conditions in Python ask exactly this: is this boolean expression True or False? The whole if/else machinery is just a way of choosing a path based on that answer.

A boolean expression can also be a variable that already holds a bool:

is_vip = True
if is_vip:
    print("VIP discount applied")
topics.title: Boolean expressions

codeExamples.explanation: The indented line runs only when marks is 70 or more.
codeExamples.title: Basic if

topics.theoryContent:
The if statement runs a block of code only when its condition is True.

age = int(input("Enter your age: "))
if age >= 18:
    print("You can vote.")

The condition is followed by a colon, and the block under it must be INDENTED (four spaces by convention). The indentation is not decoration — it defines which statements belong to the if. Python is one of the few languages where indentation is part of the grammar.

If the condition is False, the block is skipped entirely and the program continues with the next line at the outer indentation.
topics.title: if — run code only when a condition is true

codeExamples.explanation: Age decides which price is printed. One branch always runs.
codeExamples.title: if-else for ticketing

topics.theoryContent:
else runs when the if condition is False. Exactly one of the two blocks always runs — never both, never neither.

age = int(input("Enter your age: "))
if age >= 18:
    print("Adult ticket: Rs 150")
else:
    print("Child ticket: Rs 75")

Structure reminder:
- if condition:  then colon
- else:          then colon (no condition — it means "otherwise")
- indented blocks for both

This is the branch in a program: a road splits in two and the value decides which road to take.
topics.title: if-else — one path or the other

codeExamples.explanation: The first condition that matches decides the grade. 95 → A, 80 → B, 65 → C, 40 → D.

codeExamples.code:

income = 150000
sports_quota = False
if (marks >= 85 and income < 200000) or sports_quota:

else:

topics.theoryContent:
Real decisions rarely depend on one fact. Combine conditions:

and — all must be True
or  — at least one True
not — flip the result

A scholarship needs marks AND a financial need:
if marks >= 85 and family_income < 200000:
    print("Scholarship approved")

A gym membership is open to morning OR evening slots:
if slot == "morning" or slot == "evening":
    print("Slot available")

A service requires the account to be active:
if not account_active:
    print("Account suspended")

Write brackets around each comparison for clarity, and remember precedence: not binds tightest, then and, then or. When a condition mixes and/or, brackets are essential:
(marks >= 85 and family_income < 200000) or sports_quota
topics.title: Multiple conditions with and, or, not

days.description: Today we are learning Loops — while and for.
days.title: Loops — while and for

topics.theoryContent:
A program that prints one receipt is easy: three lines. A program that prints one hundred receipts is impossible to write by hand — you would paste the same lines a hundred times.

Real systems repeat work all the time:
- A payroll run calculates the salary of every employee in a company.
- A bank statement prints every transaction of the month.
- A courier system checks the status of every parcel.

LOOPS are the solution. A loop is a block of code that runs again and again. You write the repeated work ONCE, and the loop repeats it for as many items as needed — whether that is 3 or 30,000.

Python has two kinds of loop:
- while — repeat as long as a condition stays true.
- for — repeat once for every item in a collection.

Both will appear in almost every real Python program you ever read.
topics.title: Why loops exist

codeExamples.code:
counter = 1
while counter <= 5:
    print("Attempt", counter)
    counter = counter + 1
print("Done")
codeExamples.explanation: The block runs five times, then counter becomes 6 and the condition is False.
codeExamples.title: Counting with a while loop

codeExamples.code:
pin = input("Enter PIN: ")
while pin != "1234":
    print("Wrong PIN, try again.")
    pin = input("Enter PIN: ")
print("Access granted")
codeExamples.explanation: The loop keeps asking until the user types the correct PIN. No guessing how many tries are needed.
codeExamples.title: Retry until valid input

topics.theoryContent:
The while loop repeats a block AS LONG AS its condition is True.

counter = 1
while counter <= 5:
    print("Attempt", counter)
    counter = counter + 1

The flow: check the condition, run the block if True, go back and check again. The moment the condition becomes False, the loop stops and the program continues below.

A critical detail: the loop must be able to change the condition. The line counter = counter + 1 is what makes the loop end. If you forget it, counter never changes, the condition stays True, and the loop never stops — an infinite loop.

Real use: keep asking for input until the answer is valid.

pin = input("Enter PIN: ")
while pin != "1234":
    print("Wrong PIN, try again.")
    pin = input("Enter PIN: ")
topics.title: while — repeat while a condition is true

codeExamples.explanation: The loop body runs once for each name in the list.
codeExamples.title: Greeting every customer

topics.theoryContent:
The for loop visits every item in a collection, one at a time. It is used when you know the collection you want to go through.

names = ["Ravi", "Anita", "Sita"]
for name in names:
    print("Hello,", name)

The variable name takes each value in turn: first "Ravi", then "Anita", then "Sita". After the last item the loop ends.

for is the natural choice for processing a list: printing each order, checking each account, calculating each total. It is also safer than while — you cannot forget to advance it, because the list itself controls the repetition.

The companion to for is range(), covered next.
topics.title: for — repeat for every item

codeExamples.code:
for i in range(3):
    print("Processing order", i + 1)
codeExamples.explanation: range(3) gives 0,1,2; adding 1 makes the labels 1,2,3.
codeExamples.title: Repeating a fixed number of times

codeExamples.explanation: A negative step counts down: 10 down to 1, then the rocket launches.
codeExamples.title: Counting down with a step

topics.title: range() — counting with for

codeExamples.explanation: The loop prints only after finding 99, then breaks; the remaining items are never visited.
codeExamples.title: Finding the first match

topics.theoryContent:
break immediately exits the loop, jumping to the first line after it. It is used when the answer has been found and continuing is pointless.

numbers = [12, 45, 99, 7]
for n in numbers:
    if n == 99:
        print("Found it!")
        break

Once 99 is found, the loop stops — no need to check 7.

Real use: searching — the moment you find the record, stop scanning. Also for input validation loops, where break ends the loop after a successful answer.
topics.title: break — stop the loop early

codeExamples.explanation: Negative values are reported and skipped; positive values are processed normally.
codeExamples.title: Skipping invalid records

topics.title: continue — skip one iteration

codeExamples.explanation: For each row, every seat is visited. The inner loop repeats its whole cycle once per row.
codeExamples.title: Seat grid in a hall

topics.theoryContent:
A nested loop is a for or while inside another loop. The inner loop runs fully for every single step of the outer loop.

The classic example is a multiplication table: for every row (outer loop), print all the columns (inner loop).

for i in range(1, 4):
    for j in range(1, 4):
        print(i, "*", j, "=", i * j)
    print()     # blank line between tables

Trace through it: i=1, the inner loop prints 1*1, 1*2, 1*3, then a blank line. Then i=2, the inner loop runs again completely, and so on. With an outer loop of 3 steps and an inner loop of 3 steps, the inner body runs 3×3 = 9 times.

Nested loops appear whenever data has two dimensions: a grid of seats in a hall, a matrix of sales by region and month, a timetable of rooms and hours.
topics.title: Nested loops — a loop inside a loop

codeExamples.explanation: while True is always true, so the loop relies on break to end it — a valid pattern for menus and wait loops.
codeExamples.title: Deliberate infinite loop with an exit

topics.theoryContent:
An infinite loop never stops, because its condition never becomes False. The program appears to hang and the computer may slow down while the loop spins.

The classic cause: forgetting to update the variable the condition checks.

counter = 1
while counter <= 5:
    print("Attempt", counter)
    # counter never changes — the loop runs forever

If this happens to you, press Ctrl+C in the terminal to interrupt the program.

Rules to stay safe:
- In a while loop, always change the variable that the condition reads, inside the loop.
- Prefer for loops for counting — the list or range controls the repetition, so you cannot forget the advance step.
- If you deliberately write while True (always true), make sure a break inside ends it.

An infinite loop is rarely the intended logic — it is almost always a forgotten update line.
topics.title: Avoiding infinite loops

days.title: Strings

codeExamples.code:
word = "Python"
print("First:", word[0])
print("Last:", word[-1])
print("Middle:", word[2])
codeExamples.explanation: word[0] is the first character, word[-1] the last, and word[2] the third.
codeExamples.title: Reading characters with indexes

topics.theoryContent:
A string is a SEQUENCE: a row of characters in a fixed order. You can reach any single character by its position, called an INDEX.

name = "Ravi"
print(name[0])     # R
print(name[1])     # a
print(name[2])     # v
print(name[3])     # i

Indexes start at 0, never 1. The first character is [0].

Negative indexes count from the end: name[-1] is the last character (i), name[-2] the second-last (v).

len() tells you the length of the string — the number of characters:
print(len(name))   # 4

The last character is always name[len(name) - 1]. Understanding indexes is the foundation for slicing, the next topic.
topics.title: Strings are sequences of characters

codeExamples.code:
date = "2026-08-12"
year = date[:4]
month = date[5:7]
day = date[8:]
print("Year:", year)
print("Month:", month)
print("Day:", day)
codeExamples.explanation: The three slices pull out year, month and day from the fixed format YYYY-MM-DD.
codeExamples.title: Slicing a date

topics.theoryContent:
A slice extracts a range of characters. The syntax is string[start:end], where start is included and end is NOT (like range()).

msg = "Good morning"
print(msg[0:4])    # Good
print(msg[5:12])   # morning

Rules:
- msg[:4] — omitting start means "from the beginning": "Good".
- msg[5:] — omitting end means "to the end": "morning".
- msg[:]  — the whole string.
- msg[::2] — a third value is the step; this takes every 2nd character.

Slices never crash on out-of-range values — they just return whatever exists. msg[0:100] returns the whole string instead of an error.

Real use: extracting parts of fixed-format text — a date "2026-08-12" splits into year, month and day with three slices.
topics.title: Slicing — cutting out a piece of a string

codeExamples.code:
raw = input("Enter your name: ")
print("Display:", raw.title())
print("For login:", raw.lower())
codeExamples.explanation: title() makes the name presentable for display; lower() normalises it for case-insensitive comparisons.
codeExamples.title: Normalising a name

topics.theoryContent:
Strings have methods — built-in functions attached to the value. They do not change the original string; they return a NEW string, because strings are immutable.

name = "ravi kumar"
print(name.upper())      # RAVI KUMAR
print(name.lower())      # ravi kumar
print(name.title())      # Ravi Kumar
print(name.capitalize()) # Ravi kumar

Real use: names are typed inconsistently. When a customer types "rAvI kUMaR", converting to .title() gives a presentable "Ravi Kumar". Email addresses are usually compared in lowercase so "RAVI@X.COM" and "ravi@x.com" match.

A common trick for comparing answers regardless of case: .lower() == "yes".
topics.title: Changing case: upper, lower, title

codeExamples.explanation: strip removes accidental spaces, upper makes the comparison case-insensitive, then the check compares the cleaned code.
codeExamples.title: Cleaning a voucher code

topics.theoryContent:
Users paste text with stray spaces and tabs. strip() removes whitespace from both ends of a string.

code = "   ABC123   "
print(code.strip())    # ABC123

- lstrip() removes from the left only.
- rstrip() removes from the right only.

This is the first thing real systems do to raw input: clean it before storing or comparing. "ABC123 " with a trailing space is a different string than "ABC123", and comparisons silently fail — strip() prevents that class of bug.

Optionally you can strip specific characters: "xxxRavi".strip("x") removes the x characters.
topics.title: Cleaning text with strip

codeExamples.code:
email = "ravi@gmail.com"
if "@" in email:
    print("Looks like an email address")
print("Domain starts at index:", email.find("@"))
codeExamples.explanation: in checks presence; find gives the position of the @ symbol for further processing.
codeExamples.title: Checking if a domain is present

topics.theoryContent:
A program often needs to know whether text appears inside another string, and where.

msg = "Welcome to Python training"
print(msg.find("Python"))    # 11 — the position where "Python" starts
print(msg.find("Java"))      # -1 — not found
print(msg.count("o"))        # 2 — how many times "o" appears

- find(sub) returns the index of the first occurrence, or -1 if not found.
- index(sub) does the same but raises an error when not found — use find when you are not sure the text exists.
- count(sub) counts how many times the text appears.
- The in operator answers yes/no: "Python" in msg → True. This is the simplest check when you only need presence, not position.
topics.title: Searching: find, index, count, in

codeExamples.code:

codeExamples.explanation: The replacement returns a new message without touching the original string.

topics.theoryContent:
replace(old, new) returns a new string with every occurrence of old replaced by new. The original stays unchanged.

msg = "Payment of Rs 500 received"
print(msg.replace("Rs", "INR"))
# Payment of INR 500 received

replace is used for fixing data: updating old abbreviations, correcting typos, redacting parts of a message. It replaces ALL occurrences by default; pass a third argument to limit the count: msg.replace("a", "o", 1) replaces only the first a.
topics.title: replace — swapping text

topics.theoryContent:
split(sep) cuts a string into a list of pieces using a separator. join(list) does the reverse — it joins pieces into one string with a separator between them.

names = "Ravi,Anita,Sita"
parts = names.split(",")
print(parts)     # ['Ravi', 'Anita', 'Sita']

joined = " - ".join(parts)
print(joined)    # Ravi - Anita - Sita

The default split() splits on whitespace, so "Ravi Anand Kumar".split() gives ['Ravi', 'Anand', 'Kumar'].

Real use: parsing comma-separated exports (CSV), splitting a full name into parts, breaking a sentence into words. This is the first of many list operations — lists are the Day 8 topic.
topics.title: split and join — breaking text apart and putting it back

topics.theoryContent:
F-strings (formatted strings) are the modern way to build output that mixes text and variables. Put an f before the opening quote, and write {variable} where the value should go.

name = "Ravi"
bill = 1499.5
print(f"Customer {name} owes Rs {bill}")

Python replaces {name} and {bill} with their values. Compare with the comma version: f-strings let you control exactly where values land, and they convert numbers to text automatically.

Number formatting: {bill:.2f} forces two decimal places:
print(f"Total: Rs {bill:.2f}")   # Total: Rs 1499.50

Real use: every report, invoice, email and log message. Once you know f-strings you will reach for them constantly and rarely build strings with + again.
topics.title: f-strings — clean formatted output

days.title: Lists

codeExamples.code:
customers = ["Ravi", "Anita", "Sita"]
print("First:", customers[0])
print("Last:", customers[-1])
print("Total customers:", len(customers))
codeExamples.explanation: The list holds three names; indexes and len() read them the same way they read strings.
codeExamples.title: A list of customer names

topics.theoryContent:
A list is an ordered collection of values. Where a variable holds ONE value, a list holds MANY, and you reach each one by its position (index).

marks = [85, 90, 78]
print(marks[0])    # 85
print(marks[1])    # 90
print(marks[-1])   # 78 — negative indexes work like strings

A list is written with square brackets, items separated by commas. It can be empty: [] — a list you will fill later.

Lists can mix types: ["Ravi", 21, True] is legal. In real work, however, a list usually holds one kind of thing — a list of names, or a list of prices — because you almost always process them the same way.

len() gives the number of items:
print(len(marks))  # 3

The similarity to strings is not an accident: both are sequences. Everything you learned about string indexes and slicing carries over, with one crucial difference: lists can be CHANGED, strings cannot.
topics.title: Creating lists and accessing items

codeExamples.code:
queue = []
queue.append("Anita")
queue.append("Ravi")
queue.append("Sita")
print(queue)
codeExamples.explanation: The queue starts empty and gains one customer at a time with append.
codeExamples.title: A growing waiting list

topics.theoryContent:
A list grows as data arrives. Three methods handle it:

- append(item) — add one item to the end.
- insert(index, item) — add an item at a position, pushing the rest right.
- extend(other_list) — add all items of another list to the end.

shopping = []
shopping.append("milk")              # ['milk']
shopping.append("bread")             # ['milk', 'bread']
shopping.insert(1, "eggs")           # ['milk', 'eggs', 'bread']
shopping.extend(["butter", "jam"])   # ['milk', 'eggs', 'bread', 'butter', 'jam']

Real systems append constantly: every new sale, every new student, every new log line. The list starts empty and grows one item at a time as data comes in.

Do not confuse append and extend: append adds the whole argument as ONE item, so appending a list nests it; extend adds each of its items separately.
topics.title: Adding items: append, insert, extend

codeExamples.code:
tasks = ["report", "email", "meeting", "invoice"]
done = tasks.pop(1)        # remove "email" and keep it
print("Finished:", done)
print("Still to do:", tasks)
codeExamples.explanation: pop removes the item AND gives it back, so the finished task can be stored while the list shrinks.
codeExamples.title: A to-do list

topics.theoryContent:
Four ways to take items out:

- remove(value) — remove the first matching value.
- pop(index) — remove AND return the item at an index (default: last item).
- del list[index] — delete the item at an index.
- clear() — remove everything, leaving [].

orders = ["pending", "shipped", "pending", "cancelled"]
orders.remove("cancelled")     # removes the cancelled order
last = orders.pop()            # takes "pending" off the end, returns it
del orders[0]                  # deletes the first "pending"
orders.clear()                 # []

remove raises a ValueError if the value is not present — check with in first if you are unsure. pop is useful when you need the removed item, for example moving a task from a to-do list to a done list.
topics.title: Removing items: remove, pop, del, clear

codeExamples.code:
original = [1, 2, 3]
copy = original[:]
copy.append(4)
print("Original:", original)
print("Copy:", copy)
codeExamples.explanation: The slice makes a separate list, so changing the copy leaves the original untouched.
codeExamples.title: Copying a list safely

topics.theoryContent:
Lists slice exactly like strings:

names = ["Ravi", "Anita", "Sita", "Kavya"]
print(names[1:3])    # ['Anita', 'Sita']
print(names[:2])     # ['Ravi', 'Anita']
print(names[::2])    # ['Ravi', 'Sita'] — every 2nd item

A slice always produces a NEW list, which gives you a safe COPY trick: names[:] returns a full copy.

Why does copying matter? Because lists are MUTABLE — they can be changed in place. Assigning the same list to two names does NOT copy it:

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a              # b is not a copy; both names point to the SAME list
b.append(4)
print(a)           # [1, 2, 3, 4] — a changed too!

To make a real independent copy use slicing: b = a[:]. This reference behaviour is a classic source of confusion and will come up again when lists are passed to functions.
topics.title: Slicing and copying lists

codeExamples.code:
scores = [78, 95, 62, 88]
scores.sort(reverse=True)
print("Leaderboard:", scores)
codeExamples.explanation: sort with reverse=True orders from highest to lowest — a ready-made leaderboard.
codeExamples.title: Ranking players by score

topics.theoryContent:
sort() arranges the list in place (smallest to largest, or alphabetically). sorted() returns a NEW sorted list and leaves the original alone. reverse() flips the order in place.

scores = [78, 95, 62, 88]
scores.sort()
print(scores)          # [62, 78, 88, 95]
scores.reverse()
print(scores)          # [95, 88, 78, 62]

Use sorted() when you must keep the original order for something else:
names = ["Sita", "Ravi", "Anita"]
print(sorted(names))   # ['Anita', 'Ravi', 'Sita']
print(names)           # still ['Sita', 'Ravi', 'Anita']

Real use: reports sorted by date, rankings by score, directories by name. Sorting is one of the most requested features in real systems.
topics.title: Sorting and reversing

codeExamples.code:
marks = [85, 90, 78, 92]
average = sum(marks) / len(marks)
print("Total:", sum(marks))
print("Average:", average)
print("Best:", max(marks))
print("Worst:", min(marks))
codeExamples.explanation: Four built-ins replace hand-written loops for the standard class statistics.
codeExamples.title: Class average

topics.theoryContent:
Built-in functions answer common questions about a list instantly:

marks = [85, 90, 78, 92]
print(len(marks))    # 4 — how many
print(min(marks))    # 78 — the smallest
print(max(marks))    # 92 — the largest
print(sum(marks))    # 345 — the total

These four cover the majority of simple reporting needs: a class average is sum(marks) / len(marks), the best score is max(marks), the lowest is min(marks). No loop required — they are implemented in C and are fast even on large lists.

For min and max on non-numeric lists, the comparison is alphabetical: min(["apple", "banana"]) → "apple".
topics.title: len, min, max, sum — quick statistics

codeExamples.explanation: The loop tests each number and appends only the even ones, building the result list step by step.
codeExamples.title: Filtering with a loop and append

topics.theoryContent:
The in operator checks whether a value is present. The for loop visits every item.

stock = ["laptop", "mouse", "keyboard"]
print("mouse" in stock)     # True
print("printer" in stock)   # False

for item in stock:
    print("Stock:", item)

The for loop is how lists get processed in bulk — apply a check, a discount, a label to every item. Combined with append, the loop also BUILDS lists: collect only the values that pass a filter:

evens = []
for n in range(1, 11):
    if n % 2 == 0:
        evens.append(n)
print(evens)     # [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]

This collect-while-iterating pattern is one of the most common in Python.
topics.title: Membership and iterating over a list

codeExamples.code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b.append(99)
print(a)
print(b)
codeExamples.explanation: Both print the same list because a and b reference one list — appending through b changed what a sees.
codeExamples.title: Seeing the shared reference

topics.theoryContent:
Lists can be modified in place, and assigning a list does not copy it. Both facts shape how you write safe code.

Mutable means the contents can change: list[0] = "new" works, unlike a string where that would error. Real systems rely on this — a shopping cart is a list that is constantly updated.

The reference trap: when you assign a list to another name, you are NOT making a copy. Both names point to the same list. A change through one name appears through the other.

team = ["Anita"]
copy = team
copy.append("Ravi")
print(team)     # ['Anita', 'Ravi'] — same list changed!

The mental model: a variable holding a list stores a REFERENCE to the list, not the list itself. If you need an independent copy, use slicing (list[:]).
topics.title: Lists are mutable — and shared by reference

codeExamples.explanation: The three facts belong together and never change, so a tuple is the natural container.

topics.theoryContent:
A tuple is an ordered collection of values, written with round brackets:

point = (3, 4)
student = ("Ravi", 21, "CSE")

It looks almost like a list — indexes, len(), iteration and membership all work the same:

print(point[0])      # 3
print(len(student))  # 3
for value in student:
    print(value)

The ONE structural difference: a tuple cannot be changed after it is created. No append, no remove, no assigning to an index. It is immutable.

That single property makes tuples the right choice whenever the data is a fixed record: a point in space, a student roll entry, a date. Lists are for collections that grow and shrink; tuples are for fixed facts.
topics.title: What is a tuple?

codeExamples.code:
home = (10, 20)
office = (50, 80)
print(home)
print(office)
print("Office x:", office[0])
codeExamples.explanation: Each location is one tuple of two numbers — a fixed fact that will not change.
codeExamples.title: Coordinates as tuples

topics.theoryContent:
A tuple is created with round brackets and commas:

empty = ()            # an empty tuple
single = (5,)         # one item — the comma is REQUIRED
pair = (10, 20)

The trailing comma in single = (5,) is the thing beginners forget. (5) is just the number 5 in brackets; (5,) is a one-item tuple.

The comma, not the brackets, makes a tuple. You can even write a tuple without brackets:

coord = 3, 4
print(coord)     # (3, 4)

Brackets are the normal style for readability. Tuples can hold mixed types — a tuple of a name and a price is fine — and tuples can be nested: ((1, 2), (3, 4)).
topics.title: Creating tuples

codeExamples.code:
data = [1, 2, 3]
frozen = tuple(data)
print(frozen)            # (1, 2, 3)
mutable = list(frozen)
mutable.append(4)
print(mutable)           # [1, 2, 3, 4]
codeExamples.explanation: tuple() freezes a list into an unchangeable tuple; list() thaws a tuple back into a growable list.
codeExamples.title: Converting between list and tuple

topics.theoryContent:
Try to change a tuple and Python refuses:

point = (3, 4)
point[0] = 9     # TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment

point.append(5)  # AttributeError: 'tuple' object has no attribute 'append'

This is deliberate, not a limitation. Knowing a tuple cannot change guarantees safety: data can be shared and passed around without any code accidentally modifying it. If a list was shared and some other part of the program appended to it, the change would silently affect everyone using it. A tuple removes that entire class of bug.

The trade-off: if your data truly needs to grow or change, use a list. If it represents a fixed set of facts, a tuple protects it.

You can convert between them when you need the other behaviour:
mutable = list(my_tuple)
frozen = tuple(my_list)
topics.title: Immutability — you cannot change a tuple

codeExamples.code:
emp = (204, "Kavya", 28500.0)
print("ID:", emp[0])
print("Name:", emp[1])
print("Salary:", emp[2])
codeExamples.explanation: A fixed employee record read field by field with indexes.
codeExamples.title: Reading fields from a record

topics.theoryContent:
Tuples support everything sequences support — with the fixed-amount bonus:

record = (101, "Anita", "CSE", 2026)
print(record[0])     # 101
print(record[-1])    # 2026
print(record[1:3])   # ('Anita', 'CSE')
print("CSE" in record)   # True
print(len(record))   # 4

Slicing a tuple returns a new tuple. Iteration works exactly as with lists:

for field in record:
    print(field)

Since a tuple is a fixed record, the most common operations are reading fields by index and unpacking — which is the next topic.
topics.title: Indexing and slicing tuples

codeExamples.code:
record = ("Ravi", 27, "Hyderabad")
name, age, city = record
print(f"{name}, age {age}, lives in {city}")
codeExamples.explanation: One unpacking line turns the tuple into three named variables, making the code read like a sentence.
codeExamples.title: Unpacking a customer record

topics.theoryContent:
Packing is putting several values into one tuple. Unpacking is the reverse — pulling them out into separate variables in one line.

Packing happens automatically when you write values separated by commas:
details = ("Anita", 22, "Chennai")

Unpacking assigns each item to its own variable:
name, age, city = details
print(name)    # Anita
print(age)     # 22
print(city)    # Chennai

The number of variables must match the number of items. Unpacking is Python's most elegant convenience: functions that return several values (Day 20) hand them back as a tuple, and the caller unpacks them in one line.

A common real-world unpacking is splitting a full name:
full = "Ravi Kumar Reddy"
first, *rest = full.split()   # first = "Ravi", rest = ["Kumar", "Reddy"]
topics.title: Packing and unpacking

codeExamples.code:
a = 5
b = 10
a, b = b, a
print("a:", a)
print("b:", b)
codeExamples.explanation: The pair (b, a) is created first, then unpacked into a and b — the swap happens safely in one line.
codeExamples.title: Swapping two numbers

topics.theoryContent:
Swapping two variables — putting a's value into b and b's value into a — normally takes a temporary variable:

temp = a
a = b
b = temp

With tuple unpacking it is one line, because the right side is packed before the left side is unpacked:

a, b = b, a

The right-hand side (b, a) builds a tuple first; only then does unpacking assign its items. No temporary variable needed. This is a famous Python one-liner and a favorite in coding interviews.
topics.title: Swapping values the tuple way

codeExamples.code:
txn = (1001, 1499.50, "2026-08-12", "completed")
txn_id, amount, date, status = txn
print(f"Txn {txn_id}: Rs {amount} on {date} is {status}")
codeExamples.explanation: The four fields of one transaction are packed in a tuple, then unpacked into readable names for display.
codeExamples.title: A transaction as a tuple

topics.theoryContent:
Because they are immutable, tuples are the workhorse for fixed data:

- COORDINATES — map points, GPS locations: (lat, lon).
- RECORDS — one row of fixed data: (id, name, amount).
- RANGES — (start, end) for time slots, price brackets.
- MULTIPLE RETURN VALUES — a function returning (total, count).
- DICTIONARY KEYS — later, tuples can serve as keys where lists cannot (Day 10).
- SAFE SHARING — passing a tuple to a function guarantees nobody can mutate your data.

A practical rule: if the values will be read together and never individually changed, a tuple communicates "this is a fixed fact". If the collection will grow or shrink — a cart, a queue, a log — use a list.

Real example: a bank stores each transaction as a tuple (txn_id, amount, timestamp, status). The tuple guarantees that a transaction record is never accidentally altered.
topics.title: Where tuples appear in real systems

Using a list as a key — keys must be immutable.
Reading a missing key with [] and crashing; use get().
Iterating with for k in dict and expecting the value — you get the key.
Forgetting the colon in key: value pairs.
Checking existence with dict["key"] instead of in or get().

days.description: Today we are learning Dictionaries.
days.title: Dictionaries

codeExamples.explanation: Each product name maps directly to its price — no scanning needed.
codeExamples.title: A price list

topics.theoryContent:
A dictionary stores pairs of a KEY and a VALUE. A list is looked up by position (0, 1, 2…); a dictionary is looked up by name.

prices = {"laptop": 45000, "mouse": 500}
print(prices["laptop"])    # 45000
print(prices["mouse"])     # 500

The key "laptop" maps to the value 45000. The structure mirrors a real dictionary: word (key) → definition (value).

Why is this so powerful? Real data is constantly looked up by name — find the price of this product, the phone of this customer, the marks of this student. With a list you would have to scan item by item to find a match. With a dictionary the lookup by key is effectively instant, even with millions of entries.

Dictionaries are the single most used data structure in real Python systems.
topics.title: What is a dictionary?

codeExamples.explanation: The dictionary groups a student's facts, each reachable by a descriptive key.
codeExamples.title: A student record

topics.theoryContent:
A dictionary is written with curly brackets, key: value pairs separated by commas:

student = {
    "name": "Ravi",
    "age": 21,
    "branch": "CSE"
}

Read a value with the key in square brackets:
print(student["name"])     # Ravi

Keys are usually strings, but they can be numbers too: {1: "one", 2: "two"}. The value can be anything — a number, a string, a list, or even another dictionary.

One rule matters above all: keys must be UNIQUE and IMMUTABLE. You cannot have two "name" keys, and a key cannot be a list (which is changeable). Strings, numbers and tuples all work as keys.

Reading a key that does not exist raises a KeyError:
print(student["city"])     # KeyError: 'city'
The next topics show the safe ways to handle this.
topics.title: Creating dictionaries and reading values

codeExamples.code:
stock = {"laptop": 10, "mouse": 25}
stock["laptop"] -= 2          # two laptops sold
stock["printer"] = 3          # new item added
print(stock)
codeExamples.explanation: The -= updates an existing item; the plain assignment adds a new one. One syntax, two behaviours.
codeExamples.title: Updating stock levels

topics.theoryContent:
Assigning to a key does two jobs at once: if the key exists, it UPDATES the value; if it does not, it ADDS a new pair.

inventory = {"laptop": 10, "mouse": 25}

inventory["laptop"] = 8      # update: laptop now 8
inventory["keyboard"] = 15   # add: a brand new key
print(inventory)             # {'laptop': 8, 'mouse': 25, 'keyboard': 15}

The same assignment syntax covers both — Python checks whether the key exists and acts accordingly. Real systems use this constantly: a stock level goes down (update), a new product arrives (add).

Note the += shortcut works here too:
inventory["laptop"] += 2     # laptop 8 + 2 = 10
topics.title: Adding and updating entries

codeExamples.explanation: The mouse key and its value are removed from the dictionary in one statement.
codeExamples.title: Deleting an item from stock

topics.theoryContent:
Two ways to remove a pair:

del dict[key]             # delete the pair
value = dict.pop(key)     # delete AND return the value

inventory = {"laptop": 10, "mouse": 25, "printer": 3}
del inventory["mouse"]          # mouse is gone
gone = inventory.pop("printer") # gone = 3, printer removed

pop is useful when you need the value you are removing — for example archiving a record before deleting it. del is used when you just want it gone.

A missing key raises a KeyError for both, so check with in or use the safe pop:
removed = inventory.pop("unknown", None)   # returns None instead of crashing
topics.title: Removing entries

codeExamples.explanation: Present keys return their value; missing keys return the default 0 instead of crashing.
codeExamples.title: Safe stock lookup

topics.theoryContent:
Reading a missing key with brackets raises a KeyError and crashes the program. get() returns a safe default instead:

stock = {"laptop": 10}
print(stock["printer"])          # KeyError — crashes
print(stock.get("printer"))      # None — safe
print(stock.get("printer", 0))   # 0 — your chosen default

The second argument is the value returned when the key is absent. This makes get() the workhorse for safe lookups: you can look up a customer's balance, a product's price, a user's role — and get a sensible default instead of a crash when the record is missing.

Real pattern: counting with defaults.
counts = {}
counts["apple"] = counts.get("apple", 0) + 1   # first apple → 1
topics.title: get() — reading safely

codeExamples.code:
student = {"name": "Ravi", "age": 21, "branch": "CSE"}
print(list(student.keys()))
print(list(student.values()))
print(list(student.items()))
codeExamples.explanation: Converting the views to lists makes them easy to inspect and iterate.
codeExamples.title: Listing the contents

topics.theoryContent:
Three methods expose the dictionary's contents as views you can loop over or convert to a list:

student = {"name": "Ravi", "age": 21, "branch": "CSE"}

print(student.keys())     # dict_keys(['name', 'age', 'branch'])
print(student.values())   # dict_values(['Ravi', 21, 'CSE'])
print(student.items())    # dict_items([('name', 'Ravi'), ('age', 21), ('branch', 'CSE')])

- keys() — all the keys.
- values() — all the values.
- items() — the pairs, each as a (key, value) tuple.

These are live views of the dictionary, but for practical use the pattern is with for loops and with list() to convert:

print(list(student.keys()))     # ['name', 'age', 'branch']
topics.title: keys(), values(), items()

codeExamples.explanation: Each iteration unpacks one (item, qty) pair, producing a clean two-column report.
codeExamples.title: Printing an inventory report

topics.theoryContent:
The for loop gives you the keys by default. To get values or pairs, use the methods:

student = {"name": "Ravi", "age": 21, "branch": "CSE"}

for key in student:               # keys
    print(key)

for key in student.keys():        # same — keys explicitly
    print(key)

for value in student.values():    # values
    print(value)

for key, value in student.items():   # both — the classic
    print(f"{key}: {value}")

The items() form is the one you will use most: it unpacks each pair into key and value, making the loop body read naturally. Real systems iterate records this way to print reports, generate emails, and build summaries.
topics.title: Iterating a dictionary

codeExamples.explanation: For each word, get returns the running count (0 if new), 1 is added, and the result is stored back — the classic counter pattern.

days.description: Today we are learning Functions.
days.title: Functions

topics.theoryContent:
So far every program ran top to bottom, one instruction at a time. That works for small scripts, but real systems need a way to package work into named, reusable units. That is what a FUNCTION is.

Three reasons functions matter:

1. REUSE — a payroll department calculates tax every month. Write the calculation once inside a function, and every report calls it by name. Change the tax rule in one place, and every caller uses the new rule.

2. ORGANISATION — a big program becomes unreadable as one long list of lines. Functions break it into named chapters: validate_input(), calculate_total(), send_email(). A reader scans the chapter titles instead of every line.

3. ISOLATION — each function is a box. The variables inside it do not leak into the rest of the program. A bug stays inside the box it belongs to, instead of contaminating everything.

From this day on, every real program you write should be built from functions.
topics.title: Why functions exist

codeExamples.code:
def show_menu():
    print("1. View balance")
    print("2. Withdraw cash")
    print("3. Exit")

show_menu()
show_menu()
codeExamples.explanation: The body does not run when defined. It runs each time the function is called — here, twice.
codeExamples.title: Define then call

topics.theoryContent:
Define a function with the def keyword, a name, brackets, a colon, and an indented body.

def greet():
    print("Hello!")

Defining does NOT run the body. It just teaches Python the name. To actually run it you must CALL it:

greet()     # prints Hello!

Compare a function to a recipe: writing the recipe in a cookbook does not cook anything; following it does. Defining = writing the recipe. Calling = following it.

Rules for the name, like variable names: lowercase with underscores (snake_case), a verb that says what the function does — calculate_total, send_email, check_stock.
topics.title: Defining and calling a function

codeExamples.code:
def greet(name):
    print("Hello,", name)

greet("Ravi")
greet("Anita")
greet("Sita")
codeExamples.explanation: One function, three calls, three different outputs — the argument supplies the difference.
codeExamples.title: Reusable greeting

topics.theoryContent:
A function can receive data through PARAMETERS — names listed in the brackets that act like local variables filled with whatever the caller passes.

def greet(name):
    print("Hello,", name)

greet("Ravi")     # Hello, Ravi
greet("Anita")    # Hello, Anita

The same function now serves any name. The value passed at the call site is called an ARGUMENT. Parameters are the function's side of the deal; arguments are the caller's side.

Multiple parameters work the same way, one argument per parameter, in order:

def bill(item, price, qty):
    print(item, "x", qty, "=", price * qty)

bill("Laptop Stand", 1499.5, 2)

This is how functions stop repeating yourself: the variation between calls goes in the arguments; the shared logic stays in the body.
topics.title: Parameters — sending data in

codeExamples.code:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

total = add(3, 5)
print("Sum is", total)
print("Double sum is", total * 2)
codeExamples.explanation: return hands 8 back; the caller stores it and uses it in further calculations.
codeExamples.title: A function that returns

codeExamples.explanation: The first return exits immediately. The second line only runs when the condition is False.
codeExamples.title: return stops the function

topics.theoryContent:
print() shows a result on screen; return hands a result BACK to the caller so the program can use it in a calculation.

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

total = add(3, 5)     # total = 8
print(total)

The difference is the whole point of functions as building blocks: a function that returns a value plugs into the code around it like a component. calculate_total() returns the total; the caller decides what to do with it — print it, save it, or pass it to another function.

When return runs, the function ends immediately — lines after it are skipped.

A function with no return (like greet) returns None, the "nothing" value from Day 2.
topics.title: return — getting results back

codeExamples.explanation: The discount formula exists once and is applied to every bill through the loop.
codeExamples.title: One rule, many calls

topics.theoryContent:
The real payoff of functions is removing duplicated code. Compare two versions of a "20% discount" calculation.

WITHOUT functions — the rule is typed every time, and any change must be made in every copy:
total = 500
print("Pay:", total * 0.8)
total2 = 1200
print("Pay:", total2 * 0.8)
total3 = 75
print("Pay:", total3 * 0.8)

WITH one function — the rule lives in exactly one place:
def apply_discount(amount):
    return amount * 0.8

for bill in [500, 1200, 75]:
    print("Pay:", apply_discount(bill))

When the discount becomes 15%, you edit ONE line. In the first version, one forgotten copy silently charges the wrong price. Duplicated logic is not just extra typing — it is a bug waiting for the day the rule changes.
topics.title: Functions reduce repetition

codeExamples.code:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

def double(x):
    return x * 2

print("Start")
result = double(add(3, 5))
print("Result:", result)
codeExamples.explanation: The inner call add(3,5) runs first and returns 8; double(8) then returns 16. Inner calls complete before outer ones.
codeExamples.title: Tracing the jump

topics.theoryContent:
When a program runs and hits a function call, it PAUSES where it is, jumps into the function, runs its body, and returns to exactly the next line after the call — carrying the returned value.

print("Start")
result = add(3, 5)
print("Result:", result)

Trace it:
1. "Start" prints.
2. The program jumps into add with a=3, b=5.
3. add computes 8 and returns it.
4. The program lands back on the line after the call, result = 8.
5. "Result: 8" prints.

This jump-in, return-out behaviour is called the call stack. You can trace any program by following it: which line is running, which function it jumped into, and where it will return to.
topics.title: The flow of a function call

Passing arguments in the wrong order with positional calls.

Expecting a function with no return to hand back a value (it returns None).
Forgetting to unpack multiple return values: q, r = divide(17, 5).
Using *args when a normal fixed-parameter function would be clearer.

    return principal * rate * factor / (factor - 1)

monthly = emi(p, mr, m)
total = monthly * m
interest = total - p
