codeExamples.code:
def profile(name, age, city):
    print(f"{name}, {age}, from {city}")

profile("Ravi", 21, "Hyderabad")
profile("Hyderabad", "Ravi", 21)
codeExamples.explanation: The first call is correct. The second call puts the city in the name slot — no error, just nonsense data.
codeExamples.title: Order matters

topics.theoryContent:
Positional arguments are matched by ORDER: the first argument fills the first parameter, the second fills the second, and so on.

def profile(name, age, city):
    print(name, age, city)

profile("Ravi", 21, "Hyderabad")

Positional passing is simple but fragile: if the caller swaps two arguments, the values silently land in the wrong parameters — the program runs, but with wrong data. The next topic shows the safer alternative.
topics.title: Positional arguments

codeExamples.explanation: Values reach the right parameters regardless of the order written at the call site.
codeExamples.title: Calling by keyword

topics.theoryContent:
Keyword arguments pass each value by the parameter NAME, in any order:

def profile(name, age, city):
    print(f"{name}, {age}, from {city}")

profile(city="Chennai", name="Anita", age=22)

The order no longer matters — each value is matched to its named parameter directly. Keyword arguments are the professional default for functions with several parameters, because the call site reads like a sentence and cannot silently mis-order values.

You can mix them, but positional arguments must come first:
profile("Kavya", age=24, city="Mumbai")
topics.title: Keyword arguments

codeExamples.code:
def delivery_fee(distance_km, per_km=2.5):
    return distance_km * per_km

print("5 km:", delivery_fee(5))
print("5 km express:", delivery_fee(5, 5.0))
codeExamples.explanation: Normal delivery uses the default rate; express delivery overrides it with a higher rate.
codeExamples.title: Delivery fee with a default

topics.theoryContent:
A parameter can have a DEFAULT value, used when the caller does not supply one:

def discount(price, rate=0.10):
    return price * (1 - rate)

print(discount(1000))          # 900 — default 10%
print(discount(1000, 0.25))    # 750 — explicit 25%

Defaults let a function cover the common case with a short call, while still allowing special cases to override. They are everywhere in real libraries: functions that need a custom option rarely force every caller to pass it.

Rules:
- Default parameters must come after non-default ones: def f(a, b=1) is fine; def f(a=1, b) is an error.
- Defaults are evaluated once, at definition time — for simple values like numbers and strings that is exactly what you want.
topics.title: Default parameter values

codeExamples.code:
def divide(a, b):
    return a // b, a % b

q, r = divide(17, 5)
print("Quotient:", q)
print("Remainder:", r)
codeExamples.explanation: The function packs two values into a tuple; unpacking captures both into named variables.
codeExamples.title: Returning quotient and remainder

topics.theoryContent:
A function can return several values at once, packed as a tuple (Day 9). The caller unpacks them in one line:

def divide(a, b):
    quotient = a // b
    remainder = a % b
    return quotient, remainder

q, r = divide(17, 5)
print(q, r)     # 3 2

The line return quotient, remainder builds the tuple (3, 2); the caller's q, r = unpacks it. This is the standard way a function reports more than one fact — a calculation and its remainder, a result and an error flag, an item and its position.
topics.title: Returning multiple values

codeExamples.code:
bonus = 100

def pay(base):
    return base + bonus

print(pay(1000))     # 1100 — reads the global bonus
codeExamples.explanation: The function can read the global bonus but does not change it.
codeExamples.title: Reading a global

codeExamples.code:
bonus = 100

def pay(base):
    bonus = 200
    return base + bonus

print(pay(1000))     # 1200 — local bonus
print(bonus)         # 100 — global unchanged
codeExamples.explanation: bonus = 200 inside the function creates a separate local variable; the global keeps its value.
codeExamples.title: Assigning creates a local

topics.theoryContent:
SCOPE decides which variables a piece of code can see. Variables created inside a function are LOCAL — they exist only while the function runs, and no other part of the program can see them.

def add_ten(x):
    result = x + 10     # local to add_ten
    return result

add_ten(5)
print(result)     # NameError — result does not exist here

This is a feature, not a limitation. Local scope means a function cannot accidentally overwrite the variables of the caller, and two functions can both use a variable named total without interfering.

A variable defined outside all functions is GLOBAL — visible everywhere. A function can READ a global, but assigning to that name inside the function creates a NEW local instead:

bonus = 100            # global
def pay(base):
    return base + bonus   # reads the global

def pay2(base):
    bonus = 200           # new LOCAL bonus, the global is untouched
    return base + bonus

Rule of thumb: pass values into functions as parameters and get results back via return. Relying on globals inside functions makes code hard to follow — the function's behaviour then depends on hidden outside state.
topics.title: Local and global scope

codeExamples.explanation: *args packs every argument into a tuple, letting one function handle any count.

days.title: Sets

codeExamples.code:
emails = ["ravi@x.com", "anita@x.com", "ravi@x.com"]
unique = set(emails)
print(unique)
print("Count:", len(unique))
codeExamples.explanation: Building a set from a list removes duplicates automatically — 3 entries become 2.
codeExamples.title: Duplicates vanish

topics.theoryContent:
A set is an unordered collection of UNIQUE items. Three properties define it:

1. NO DUPLICATES — each item appears at most once.
2. UNORDERED — there is no index; items have no position you can rely on.
3. FAST MEMBERSHIP — checking whether an item is in the set is effectively instant, even with millions of items.

You write a set with curly brackets:
active_users = {"Ravi", "Anita", "Sita"}

The uniqueness is automatic — building a set from a list with duplicates removes them:
print(set([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]))    # {1, 2, 3}

Real systems use sets wherever duplicates must be prevented or removed: registered emails, allocated seats, visited pages, voter lists.
topics.title: What is a set?

codeExamples.code:
empty_set = set()
empty_dict = {}
print(type(empty_set))
print(type(empty_dict))
codeExamples.explanation: set() gives a set; {} gives a dictionary. The two look similar but are different types.
codeExamples.title: Empty set vs empty dict

topics.theoryContent:
Create a set with curly brackets or with the set() constructor:

s1 = {"apple", "banana"}          # literal
s2 = set(["apple", "banana"])     # from a list
empty = set()                     # an empty set

Watch the trap: {} creates an empty DICTIONARY, not a set. To make an empty set you must write set().

Set items must be immutable — numbers, strings and tuples are fine; lists are not (a list could change, breaking the set's uniqueness guarantee).

And remember: no duplicates allowed. Writing {"a", "a", "b"} silently keeps one "a".
topics.title: Creating sets

codeExamples.code:
attendees = {"Ravi", "Anita"}
attendees.add("Sita")
attendees.add("Ravi")          # duplicate — ignored
attendees.discard("Kavya")     # not present — no error
print(attendees)
codeExamples.explanation: add ignores duplicates, discard is safe on missing values, and the set always holds unique names.
codeExamples.title: Managing an attendee set

topics.title: Adding and removing elements

codeExamples.explanation: Three operators answer the three questions about the two lists instantly.
codeExamples.title: Comparing two attendance lists

topics.theoryContent:
The real power of sets is comparing collections. Three operations cover most needs:

UNION (|) — everything from both sets.
INTERSECTION (&) — items in BOTH sets.
DIFFERENCE (-) — items in the first set but not the second.

morning = {"Ravi", "Anita"}
evening = {"Anita", "Sita"}

print(morning | evening)    # {'Ravi', 'Anita', 'Sita'} — everyone
print(morning & evening)    # {'Anita'} — came to both
print(morning - evening)    # {'Ravi'} — only morning
print(evening - morning)    # {'Sita'} — only evening

Real use: which customers bought in both months (intersection), which joined last month but not this one (difference), the full customer base (union). These are one-liners that would otherwise need slow nested loops.
topics.title: Union, intersection, difference

codeExamples.explanation: One in check on a set answers the question instantly and cleanly.
codeExamples.title: Instant membership check

topics.theoryContent:
The in operator on a set is what makes sets famous: it is fast regardless of set size.

registered = {"ravi@x.com", "anita@x.com"}
print("ravi@x.com" in registered)     # True
print("new@x.com" in registered)      # False

With a list of the same data, Python would scan item by item until it finds a match. With a set, it jumps straight to the answer. When you only need "is this present?" and not a position, a set is the right tool.

Iteration works with a for loop, but the order is not guaranteed:

for name in registered:
    print(name)

If you need a predictable order, convert to a sorted list: sorted(registered).
topics.title: Membership and iteration

codeExamples.code:
raw = ["a", "b", "a", "c", "b"]
seen = set()
ordered = []
for item in raw:
    if item not in seen:
        seen.add(item)
        ordered.append(item)
print(ordered)
codeExamples.explanation: The set tracks what has been seen; the list keeps the first-appearance order — the classic dedupe pipeline.
codeExamples.title: Deduplicating while keeping order

topics.theoryContent:
Lists and sets overlap, so the choice comes down to what the program needs:

USE A LIST when:
- Order matters (a queue, a top-10, a timeline).
- Duplicates must be preserved (a cart with two of the same item).
- You need the item at a position (list[3]).

USE A SET when:
- Duplicates must be prevented or removed.
- You only ask "is it present?" — membership checks.
- You need to compare two collections (union, intersection, difference).
- Order does not matter.

A common pipeline: collect items in a list as they arrive (preserving order), then convert to a set when you need to deduplicate or compare. set() and list() convert freely in both directions.
topics.title: Sets vs lists — which to use

codeExamples.code:
squares = [n * n for n in range(1, 6)]
print(squares)
codeExamples.explanation: The comprehension builds [1, 4, 9, 16, 25] in a single expression — the loop is implicit.
codeExamples.title: Squares in one line

topics.theoryContent:
Day 8 showed the collect-while-iterating pattern: start with an empty list, loop, and append the values you want.

squares = []
for n in range(1, 6):
    squares.append(n * n)
print(squares)     # [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]

This pattern is so common that Python has a one-line shorthand for it, called a LIST COMPREHENSION:

squares = [n * n for n in range(1, 6)]
print(squares)     # [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]

Read it like a sentence: "make a list of n*n, for each n in range(1, 6)". The structure is:

[ expression  for item in collection ]

- expression — what each result looks like.
- for item in collection — the iteration that supplies the values.

Every time you find yourself writing "start a list, loop, append", consider replacing it with a comprehension.
topics.title: The pattern: collect while iterating

codeExamples.code:
names = ["Ravi", "Anita", "Sita", "Kavya"]
short = [n.upper() for n in names if len(n) <= 4]
print(short)
codeExamples.explanation: Only names of length 4 or less are kept, and each kept name is uppercased.
codeExamples.title: Filter and transform together

topics.theoryContent:
Add an if at the end to keep only the items that pass the test:

evens = [n for n in range(1, 11) if n % 2 == 0]
print(evens)     # [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]

Structure with a filter:
[ expression  for item in collection  if condition ]

The comprehension is a compact version of the classic loop:
evens = []
for n in range(1, 11):
    if n % 2 == 0:
        evens.append(n)

The if decides which items are processed; the expression decides what each kept item becomes. You can combine both — filter AND transform:

names = ["Ravi", "Anita", "Sita", "Kavya"]
short = [n.upper() for n in names if len(n) <= 4]
print(short)     # ['RAVI', 'SITA']
topics.title: Filtering with if

codeExamples.code:
prices = [100, 250, 400]
with_tax = [round(p * 1.18, 2) for p in prices]
print(with_tax)
codeExamples.explanation: Each price is transformed by the expression; the result is a new list of taxed amounts.
codeExamples.title: Applying tax to a price list

topics.theoryContent:
The expression on the left can be any calculation — it just produces the values that go into the result list.

prices = [100, 250, 400]
with_tax = [p * 1.18 for p in prices]
print(with_tax)    # [118.0, 295.0, 472.0]

words = "apple banana apple grape".split()
lens = [len(w) for w in words]
print(lens)        # [5, 6, 5, 5]

marks = [85, 90, 78, 92]
passed = [m for m in marks if m >= 40]
print(passed)      # [85, 90, 78, 92]

A comprehension reads best when it is short enough to fit one mental breath. When the logic grows long, go back to a plain loop with a clear name — a readable loop beats a clever one-liner nobody can parse.
topics.title: Using expressions in comprehensions

codeExamples.explanation: Each name becomes a key and its length the value — a dictionary built in one expression.
codeExamples.title: Building a name → length dictionary

topics.title: Comprehensions for other collections

codeExamples.code:
seats = [f"R{r}-S{s}" for r in range(1, 3) for s in range(1, 3)]
print(seats)
codeExamples.explanation: The outer loop over rows runs first, the inner over seats — producing every combination.

topics.theoryContent:
A comprehension can contain a second for loop, creating the flattened result of nested iteration:

pairs = [f"{i}-{j}" for i in range(1, 3) for j in range(1, 3)]
print(pairs)     # ['1-1', '1-2', '2-1', '2-2']

Trace the order: the FIRST for is the outer loop, the SECOND is the inner loop — same nesting as a loop inside a loop.

Nested comprehensions are powerful but quickly become unreadable beyond two levels. The professional rule: use one level freely, and if you need two or more, a plain nested loop with clear names is usually the better choice.

codeExamples.code:
import math
print(math.sqrt(144))
print(math.pi)
codeExamples.explanation: import math loads the toolbox; math.sqrt and math.pi use two of its tools.
codeExamples.title: Using a standard library module

topics.theoryContent:
A module is a Python file containing functions and values that you can REUSE from other programs. The standard library is the huge collection of modules that ships with Python — ready-made solutions for maths, dates, files, web requests, randomness and hundreds more.

Instead of writing everything from scratch, real developers import what they need:
- math — advanced maths functions.
- random — random numbers and choices.
- datetime — working with dates and times.
- statistics — mean, median, standard deviation.
- os — files and folders on the computer.

A module is like a toolbox: importing it puts the toolbox on the bench, and you take out only the tools you need. Modules are the reason "don't rebuild what exists" is practical.
topics.title: What is a module?

codeExamples.code:
import random
dice = random.randint(1, 6)
print("You rolled:", dice)
codeExamples.explanation: random.randint returns a random whole number between the two arguments, inclusive.
codeExamples.title: A dice roll

topics.theoryContent:
The import statement loads a module so its names are available under the module name:

import math
import random

print(math.floor(4.7))     # 4
print(random.randint(1, 6))    # a random number 1-6

After import math, every tool is reached as math.NAME. The module name acts as a namespace — a folder that keeps its functions from clashing with yours.

You can import several modules in one line or separate lines; separate lines are the usual style:
import math
import random
topics.title: import — loading a module

codeExamples.code:
from math import floor
print(floor(4.7))
codeExamples.explanation: floor is imported directly, so no math. prefix is needed when calling it.
codeExamples.title: Direct import of a function

topics.theoryContent:
from module import name pulls a single tool into your program directly, so you call it without the module prefix:

from math import sqrt, pi

print(sqrt(16))    # 4.0 — no math. prefix needed
print(pi)          # 3.141592653589793

Trade-off: it is shorter to type, but the imported name now lives in your namespace. If your program already has a variable named pi, the import quietly overwrites it. For this reason most professional code prefers import math and math.pi — the prefix keeps every use explicit and traceable.

from math import * imports everything and is generally avoided — it dumps every name into your namespace and makes collisions much more likely.
topics.title: from ... import — importing specific names

codeExamples.code:
import statistics as st
marks = [72, 85, 91, 60]
print("Mean:", st.mean(marks))
print("Median:", st.median(marks))
codeExamples.explanation: st.mean and st.median compute the average and the middle value of the marks.
codeExamples.title: Aliasing statistics

topics.theoryContent:
import module as alias lets you refer to the module by a shorter name:

import statistics as st

data = [70, 80, 90]
print(st.mean(data))     # 80.0

The alias is purely local — it does not change the module itself. It is used for modules with long names (or long conventions) so the code stays readable.

The most famous alias in Python is numpy's:
import numpy as np

Even when you do not use aliases much, you will meet them constantly in real code, so the pattern must be familiar.
topics.title: import ... as — giving a module a shorter name

codeExamples.code:
import random
names = ["Ravi", "Anita", "Sita", "Kavya"]
winner = random.choice(names)
print("Winner:", winner)
codeExamples.explanation: random.choice picks one random item from the list — a ready-made draw.
codeExamples.title: Random prize selection

topics.theoryContent:
Five modules cover most everyday needs:

math — functions and constants:
import math
math.sqrt(81)         # 9.0
math.factorial(5)     # 120
math.pi               # 3.14159...

random — choices and shuffles:
import random
random.randint(1, 10)      # random int in range
random.choice(["A", "B", "C"])  # random item from a list
random.shuffle(names)      # rearranges a list in place

datetime — dates and times:
import datetime
datetime.date.today()      # today's date

statistics — summary numbers:
import statistics as st
st.mean(data), st.median(data)

os — the computer's files and folders:
import os
os.listdir(".")            # files in the current folder

You do not need to memorise them. The skill is knowing they EXIST, so when a problem needs a random number or a median, you search the docs instead of writing it from scratch.
topics.title: The most useful standard library modules

codeExamples.code:
import helpers
total = 1000

topics.theoryContent:
Any .py file can be a module. Put functions in a file, and other programs can import them.

Create a file helpers.py:
# helpers.py
def discount(price, rate=0.10):
    return price * (1 - rate)

def tax(amount, rate=0.18):
    return amount * rate

Then use it from another file in the same folder:
# main.py
import helpers

total = 1000
print(helpers.tax(total))     # 180.0
print(helpers.discount(total))  # 900.0

This is how large projects organise code: related functions live in the same module, and each program imports exactly the modules it needs. When a rule changes, you edit the module once and every program that imports it picks up the change.

One caution: when you import a module, Python RUNS it top to bottom. Keep module files as definitions only, and guard any test code under if __name__ == "__main__": so it does not run on import.

days.title: Exception Handling

codeExamples.code:
age = int(input("Enter your age: "))
print("Age:", age)
print("This line never runs on bad input")
codeExamples.explanation: Typing "twenty" raises ValueError and the program stops before the last line.
codeExamples.title: An unhandled error crashes the program

topics.theoryContent:
So far, an error stopped the program. When a program crashes, Python raises an EXCEPTION — an event that says "something went wrong here". The program halts unless something catches the exception.

Errors you have already met are exceptions:
- ZeroDivisionError — dividing by zero.
- ValueError — int("abc") got text that is not a number.
- TypeError — adding a string and a number.
- KeyError — reading a missing dictionary key.
- NameError — using a variable that does not exist.

In small scripts a crash is annoying but harmless. In real systems it is dangerous: a payment program that crashes mid-transfer may leave money taken but not credited. Exception handling is how a program responds to a problem gracefully — report it, retry it, or fail safely — instead of dying.
topics.title: What is an exception?

codeExamples.explanation: Only the risky line is inside try; the except block handles exactly the expected error.
codeExamples.title: Catching bad number input

topics.theoryContent:
Wrap the risky code in try, and handle the problem in except:

try:
    age = int(input("Enter your age: "))
    print("Age:", age)
except ValueError:
    print("That is not a valid number.")

Now a bad input does not crash the program — the except block catches the error and the program continues.

try:  the code that might fail.
except:  what to do when it fails.

You can catch more than one type by naming several exceptions:
except (ValueError, TypeError):

Or catch everything (generally bad practice — it hides bugs):
except:
    print("Something went wrong.")

Catch the SPECIFIC exceptions you expect. A blanket except swallows genuine bugs and makes them silent.
topics.title: try / except — catching errors

codeExamples.explanation: Each failure type gets its own message; the program keeps running either way.
codeExamples.title: Two specific handlers

topics.theoryContent:
When several things can fail in one block, give each exception its own handler:

try:
    num = int(input("Enter a number: "))
    result = 100 / num
    print("Result:", result)
except ValueError:
    print("That was not a number.")
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("You cannot divide by zero.")

Typing "abc" hits the ValueError handler. Typing 0 hits the ZeroDivisionError handler. Python checks the handlers top to bottom and runs the first that matches.

Order matters: list the most specific exceptions first. A later except Exception: (the parent of most errors) would catch everything after it is reached, so put the general catch LAST.
topics.title: Handling different errors differently

codeExamples.explanation: else runs on success only; finally always runs, so "Done." prints in every case.
codeExamples.title: else and finally together

topics.theoryContent:
Two more clauses refine try/except:

else — runs only when NO exception happened.
finally — ALWAYS runs, whether an exception happened or not.

try:
    num = int(input("Enter a number: "))
    total = 100 / num
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("Cannot divide by zero.")
else:
    print("Result:", total)     # only when division succeeded
finally:
    print("Calculation attempted.")   # always

else is for the "happy path" work that should not happen when something failed. finally is for clean-up that must happen no matter what — closing a file, releasing a connection, saving a log line. Even if an exception escapes and the program crashes, finally still runs.
topics.title: else and finally

codeExamples.explanation: The function raises when the withdrawal is impossible; the caller catches and reports it.
codeExamples.title: Raising for invalid input

codeExamples.explanation: When n hits 0, the traceback points to line 3 and names ZeroDivisionError.
codeExamples.title: A traceback shows the exact spot

topics.theoryContent:
When an exception is NOT caught, Python prints a TRACEBACK — the trail of where the error happened. Reading it is a core skill.

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 3, in <module>
    result = 100 / num
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

Read it bottom-up:
1. The LAST line names the exception: ZeroDivisionError.
2. The lines above show the call trail: file, line number, and the code that failed.
3. The message ("division by zero") explains the specific problem.

When a program you wrote crashes, the traceback tells you the file, the line, and the operation — exactly what to fix. Never ignore the traceback; it is the error's own confession.
topics.title: The traceback — reading an error

days.title: File Handling

topics.theoryContent:
So far every value a program created vanished when it finished. Real systems must PERSIST data — save it somewhere it survives between runs:
- A library's catalogue must still exist tomorrow.
- A hotel's bookings must not vanish at midnight.
- A bank's transactions must last for years.

FILES are the simplest form of persistence: a named container on the disk. The pattern is always the same:

1. OPEN the file.
2. READ from it or WRITE to it.
3. CLOSE the file.

Modern Python mostly uses the with statement, which closes files automatically — you will meet both styles today. Everything you learn here generalises to databases later; files are the foundation.
topics.title: Why programs need files

codeExamples.code:
file = open("notes.txt", "r")
content = file.read()
print(content)
file.close()
codeExamples.explanation: open, read, close — the classic three steps. If notes.txt is missing, open raises FileNotFoundError.
codeExamples.title: Reading a file manually

topics.theoryContent:
The open() function connects your program to a file. It returns a FILE OBJECT.

file = open("data.txt", "r")   # r = read mode
content = file.read()          # read the whole file
print(content)
file.close()                   # release the file

The second argument is the MODE:
- "r" — read (the default). Fails if the file does not exist.
- "w" — write. Creates the file, or TRUNCATES it (erases existing content!).
- "a" — append. Adds to the end, keeping existing content.
- "r+" — read and write.

Closing is not optional polish — it frees the file so other programs can use it, and with write mode it makes sure the data is flushed to disk. Forgetting to close leads to locked files and lost data.

The modern, safer way is the with statement, covered next.
topics.title: Opening and closing files

codeExamples.code:
with open("notes.txt", "r") as file:
    content = file.read()
    print(content)
codeExamples.explanation: The file closes automatically when the indented block ends — no close() call needed.
codeExamples.title: Reading with with

topics.theoryContent:
The with statement opens a file and guarantees it closes — even if an error happens in between. It is the professional standard:

with open("data.txt", "r") as file:
    content = file.read()
    print(content)
# file is already closed here — no close() needed

Read it as: "with this file open, do this block". When the block ends — normally or by an error — Python closes the file automatically. You cannot forget to close.

The same works for writing:
with open("output.txt", "w") as file:
    file.write("Hello file!")

If the file does not exist in read mode, FileNotFoundError is raised. For real programs, wrap file access in try/except (Day 16) so a missing file becomes a friendly message, not a crash.
topics.title: with — files that close themselves

codeExamples.explanation: Each line is visited in turn and its newline is removed before printing.
codeExamples.title: Processing a file line by line

topics.theoryContent:
Reading the whole file is fine for small files. For logs, reports or data exports with thousands of lines, read line by line so memory stays small:

with open("marks.txt", "r") as file:
    for line in file:
        print(line.strip())

The for loop visits one line at a time; the file streams them from disk instead of loading everything at once. strip() removes the trailing newline each line carries.

readlines() returns a list of all lines — convenient but it loads the whole file:
lines = file.readlines()

And readline() reads a single line, advancing a position pointer — useful when you want lines one at a time by hand.

The line-by-line for loop is what you will use for most real file processing.
topics.title: Reading line by line

codeExamples.code:
with open("report.txt", "w") as file:
    file.write("Sales report
")
    file.write("Total: Rs 25000
")
print("Report saved.")
codeExamples.explanation:
Each write call adds text; the 
 moves to the next line. "w" starts a fresh file.
codeExamples.title: Writing a report

topics.theoryContent:
write() sends text to a file. In "w" mode the file is created or emptied first; in "a" mode the text is added to the end.

with open("report.txt", "w") as file:
    file.write("Sales report
")
    file.write("Total: Rs 25000
")

The 
 is a newline character — write() does not add one for you, so you must include it to start a new line. Compare with print(), which adds it automatically.

Watch the mode carefully:
- "w" every run starts fresh — previous content is gone.
- "a" every run adds to whatever is there.

A classic bug: opening with "w" when you meant "a", silently erasing a file you wanted to keep.
topics.title: Writing to files

codeExamples.code:
with open("audit.log", "a") as file:
    file.write("2026-08-12: sale of Rs 450
")
    file.write("2026-08-12: sale of Rs 120
")
codeExamples.explanation: Both lines are added to the end of audit.log; earlier content is preserved.
codeExamples.title: Building an audit log

topics.theoryContent:
Append mode ("a") adds content to the END of a file, preserving what is already there. This is how logs, histories and audit trails grow:

with open("audit.log", "a") as file:
    file.write("2026-08-12: withdrawal of Rs 500
")
    file.write("2026-08-12: deposit of Rs 1000
")

Every run adds lines without touching the earlier ones. If the file does not exist, "a" creates it.

Real use: a bank appends every transaction, a shop appends every sale, a system appends every error. The audit trail is built one appended line at a time — and this is exactly the file your Day 16 finally clause would write to.
topics.title: Appending to files

codeExamples.explanation: A missing file is caught and reported; the program keeps running.
codeExamples.title: Missing file handled gracefully

topics.theoryContent:
Files fail in predictable ways, and real programs handle them instead of crashing:

- FileNotFoundError — reading a file that does not exist.
- PermissionError — no right to read or write the file.
- IsADirectoryError — trying to read a folder as a file.

Wrap file access in try/except:

try:
    with open("data.txt", "r") as file:
        print(file.read())
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("The file data.txt was not found.")

The combination is the professional pattern: with guarantees the file closes, except turns the failure into a clear message. Every file your program reads in production should be treated this way.
topics.title: Handling file errors

codeExamples.code:
class Student:
    pass

s1 = Student()
s2 = Student()
print(type(s1))
codeExamples.explanation: Student is the blueprint; s1 and s2 are two separate objects built from it.
codeExamples.title: Blueprint vs building

topics.theoryContent:
So far you have built programs from functions that operate on data. OOP turns that around: it pairs DATA and the FUNCTIONS that work on it into a single unit called an OBJECT.

Think of a bank account in real life. It has data — account number, holder, balance — and it has operations — deposit, withdraw, check balance. The data and operations belong together. OOP packages them into one Account object, and the object itself refuses impossible operations (no withdrawing more than the balance).

OOP models the real world directly: a customer, an order, a car, a ticket — each becomes an object carrying its own data and behaviour. Three ideas make it work:

- CLASS — the blueprint or template.
- OBJECT — a concrete instance built from the blueprint.
- The operations defined on the class become METHODS — functions that belong to the object.

The class defines what a thing IS; the object is one actual thing.
topics.title: What is object-oriented programming?

codeExamples.explanation: The method is defined with self; calling it on an object runs it for that object.
codeExamples.title: A class with a method

topics.theoryContent:
Define a class with the class keyword and a name (in CapitalCase by convention):

class Student:
    pass

The pass keyword is a placeholder — an empty body is not allowed in Python, and pass says "nothing yet".

A class body usually holds two kinds of things:
- ATTRIBUTES — data (name, age, marks).
- METHODS — behaviour (calculate_average, has_passed).

Inside the class, attributes are accessed with self.name and methods are functions whose first parameter is self.

A real class:

class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, marks):
        self.name = name
        self.marks = marks

The __init__ method (pronounced "dunder init") is the constructor-like initialiser that sets up each new object — covered next.
topics.title: Defining a class

codeExamples.code:
class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, branch):
        self.name = name
        self.branch = branch

s1 = Student("Ravi", "CSE")
s2 = Student("Anita", "ECE")
print(s1.name, s1.branch)
print(s2.name, s2.branch)
codeExamples.explanation: Each object stores its own copies of name and branch, filled by __init__ at creation.
codeExamples.title: Objects with their own data

topics.theoryContent:
__init__ runs automatically the moment an object is created. Its job: set the starting values of the object's attributes.

class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, branch):
        self.name = name
        self.branch = branch

s1 = Student("Ravi", "CSE")
print(s1.name)      # Ravi
print(s1.branch)    # CSE

When Student("Ravi", "CSE") runs, Python:
1. Creates an empty Student object.
2. Calls __init__ on it, passing "Ravi" and "CSE" after self.
3. Inside, self.name = name stores the value ON the object.

The name __init__ is special — you never call it yourself; Python calls it for you. It is the most common special (dunder) method, and you will meet more of them on Day 20.
topics.title: __init__ — setting up new objects

codeExamples.explanation: self keeps each method bound to its own object — a1.deposit only changes a1.
codeExamples.title: Two accounts, independent data

topics.theoryContent:
self is the first parameter of every method. It refers to THE OBJECT the method was called on. It is how a method reads and changes THAT object's data.

class BankAccount:
    def __init__(self, balance):
        self.balance = balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        self.balance = self.balance + amount

a1 = BankAccount(1000)
a2 = BankAccount(500)
a1.deposit(200)

print(a1.balance)    # 1200 — only a1 changed
print(a2.balance)    # 500 — a2 untouched

Calling a1.deposit(200) is Python's way of writing BankAccount.deposit(a1, 200) — the object goes in as self. That is why self.balance refers to a1's balance, never a2's. The magic is the rule: every method's first parameter is the object it runs on.
topics.title: self — the object talking about itself

codeExamples.explanation: passed() reuses average() through self — behaviour is written once and composed.

topics.title: Methods — behaviour attached to objects

codeExamples.explanation: The class builds many objects; a list holds them, and each keeps its own movie and seat.
codeExamples.title: A list of ticket objects

topics.theoryContent:
One class can produce as many independent objects as you need — this is the point of a blueprint:

class Ticket:
    def __init__(self, movie, seat):
        self.movie = movie
        self.seat = seat

t1 = Ticket("Inception", "A12")
t2 = Ticket("Dune", "B07")
t3 = Ticket("Inception", "A13")

Each ticket has its own movie and seat; changing t1.seat never touches t2 or t3. Objects do not interfere.

Real systems create thousands of objects from one class — every transaction, every student, every order is an object built from the same class, each carrying its own data. A list of objects is the natural collection:

tickets = [Ticket("Inception", "A12"), Ticket("Dune", "B07")]
for t in tickets:
    print(t.movie, t.seat)
topics.title: Multiple objects from one class

codeExamples.explanation: Car(Vehicle) inherits start() — the child defines nothing and still has the parent's method.
codeExamples.title: Parent and child

topics.theoryContent:
Inheritance lets a new class take the attributes and methods of an existing class, then add or change what it needs. The existing class is the PARENT (or base) class; the new one is the CHILD (or derived) class.

Real example: a transport company has a general Vehicle class with methods start() and stop(). It then needs Car and Bus. Both are vehicles — they share start and stop — but Car has airbags and Bus has seat-count. Instead of copying Vehicle's methods into both, Car and Bus INHERIT from Vehicle and add only what is different.

The benefit is the same as functions: shared behaviour is written once in the parent and automatically available in every child. Changing start() in the parent updates every vehicle type.

days.title: OOP — Encapsulation and Special Methods

codeExamples.explanation: The underscore marks _balance as protected; deposit() enforces the rule, so an invalid amount is rejected.
codeExamples.title: Rules enforced inside the class

topics.theoryContent:
ENCAPSULATION means an object keeps its internal data private and controls how the outside world reads and changes it. The object is the only one who decides what is allowed.

Why does this matter? Consider a BankAccount where the outside code can do anything:

account.balance = -5000     # the code outside did this directly

Now the balance is negative and the business rule "balance cannot go negative" is violated, because the attribute was public and changeable from anywhere. Encapsulation fixes this: instead of letting code touch balance directly, the class exposes controlled methods — withdraw() checks the rule, deposit() checks the amount.

The pattern: attributes stay "private" (by convention, a leading underscore: self._balance), and the class exposes methods or properties as the only gateway. Data is protected; rules live in one place.
topics.title: What is encapsulation?

codeExamples.explanation: The underscore signals privacy; the class exposes salary() as the sanctioned way to read it.
codeExamples.title: Protected attribute by convention

topics.theoryContent:
Python does not truly hide attributes, but it has a STRONG CONVENTION: a name with a leading underscore (_balance) means "private — do not touch from outside". Honouring it is part of professional discipline.

class Employee:
    def __init__(self, name, salary):
        self._name = name
        self._salary = salary

Outside code reads the value only through the class's own methods, never directly. The underscore is a warning sign, not a lock:

- self._balance — protected. Do not use outside the class.
- self.__balance (double underscore) — name-mangled, harder to reach accidentally.

Rules of thumb:
- Public data that can change freely: plain name (self.balance).
- Data that has rules: protected _name, accessed via methods/properties.
- The double-underscore form is used rarely — the single underscore convention covers almost all real needs.
topics.title: Private attributes — the underscore convention

codeExamples.explanation: The setter runs on assignment; a negative value raises instead of corrupting the account.
codeExamples.title: A guarded property

codeExamples.explanation: The default object address is replaced by the readable string returned by __str__.
codeExamples.title: A readable __str__

topics.theoryContent:
Printing an object by default shows something useless like <__main__.Student object at 0x...>. The special method __str__ fixes that — it defines how the object looks as a STRING:

class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, marks):
        self.name = name
        self.marks = marks

    def __str__(self):
        return f"Student {self.name}: {self.marks} marks"

s = Student("Ravi", [70, 80])
print(s)     # Student Ravi: [70, 80] marks

__str__ is called by print() and str(). It exists to give HUMANS a readable description.

__repr__ is the "representation" used by the interpreter and debugging tools; when only __repr__ exists, print() falls back to it. Convention: __repr__ aims to be unambiguous (often enough to recreate the object), __str__ aims to be pretty. For this course, defining __str__ covers most needs.
topics.title: __str__ and __repr__ — how objects print

codeExamples.explanation: __eq__ decides the comparison: same name and marks means equal, even though they are different objects.
codeExamples.title: Content-based equality

topics.theoryContent:
Two objects from the same class are DIFFERENT objects even with identical data. Without __eq__, the == operator checks identity:

class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, marks):
        self.name = name
        self.marks = marks

a = Student("Ravi", [70])
b = Student("Ravi", [70])
print(a == b)     # False — two different objects

Define __eq__ to say what "equal" means for your objects:

class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, marks):
        self.name = name
        self.marks = marks
    def __eq__(self, other):
        return self.name == other.name and self.marks == other.marks

print(a == b)     # True — same name and marks

This is how real systems decide "is this the same record" — by content, not by memory location. Search results, invoice matching, and duplicate detection all rely on a well-defined __eq__.
topics.title: __eq__ — comparing objects fairly

codeExamples.code:
class Company:
    tax_rate = 0.18
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

c1 = Company("TechCo")
print(c1.name, c1.tax_rate)
print(Company.tax_rate)
codeExamples.explanation: tax_rate lives once on the class; name lives separately on each instance.
codeExamples.title: Shared vs per-object data

topics.theoryContent:
ATTRIBUTES stored on self belong to each INSTANCE. Attributes defined directly in the class body are CLASS attributes — shared by all instances.

class Company:
    tax_rate = 0.18        # class attribute — shared

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name    # instance attribute — per object

c1 = Company("TechCo")
c2 = Company("SoftCo")
print(c1.tax_rate, c2.tax_rate, Company.tax_rate)   # all 0.18

Class attributes are for values every instance shares and that are unlikely to change per instance: tax rates, conversion factors, allowed categories.

Instance attributes are for data unique to each object: name, balance, marks.

If an instance assigns to the class-attribute name (c1.tax_rate = 0.2), it creates a NEW instance attribute that shadows the shared one for c1 only — c2 still sees 0.18. Class attributes are read through instances but changed through the class.
topics.title: Class attributes vs instance attributes

days.description: Today we are learning Lambda Functions.
days.title: Lambda Functions

codeExamples.code:
double = lambda x: x * 2
print(double(5))
print(double(21))
codeExamples.explanation: double behaves like a function; the lambda body x * 2 is the return value.
codeExamples.title: A lambda in a variable

topics.theoryContent:
A LAMBDA is a function written in one expression, without a def, a name, or a body block. It is useful when you need a tiny function for a single purpose and giving it a name would be noise.

Named function:
def double(x):
    return x * 2

The same as a lambda:
double = lambda x: x * 2

The syntax: lambda parameters: expression
- lambda — the keyword.
- parameters — comma-separated (can be empty).
- the expression — evaluated and returned automatically (no return keyword).

A lambda is not magic — it IS a function. But it has exactly one expression, and that expression is what it returns.
topics.title: What is a lambda?

codeExamples.code:
names = ["Ravi", "Anita", "Sita"]
print(sorted(names, key=lambda w: w[-1]))
codeExamples.explanation: The lambda gives sorted the comparison rule without a separate def.
codeExamples.title: Sorting by last letter

topics.theoryContent:
Many Python tools take a FUNCTION as an argument. Consider sorted() — it sorts, but what if you want to sort by something other than the value itself? sorted accepts a key= argument that is a function applied to each item before comparing.

def last_letter(word):
    return word[-1]

names = ["Ravi", "Anita", "Sita"]
print(sorted(names, key=last_letter))   # sort by last letter

You just wrote a whole def for one tiny rule. A lambda makes it inline:

names = ["Ravi", "Anita", "Sita"]
print(sorted(names, key=lambda w: w[-1]))

The lambda IS the key function, defined exactly where it is used. No named helper cluttering the file. This is the pattern lambdas are made for: a small function used once, passed straight into a call.
topics.title: The problem lambdas solve

codeExamples.code:
employees = [("Ravi", 50000), ("Anita", 90000), ("Sita", 65000)]
by_salary = sorted(employees, key=lambda e: e[1])
print(by_salary)
codeExamples.explanation: Each tuple is passed to the lambda, which returns the second element — the salary — as the sort key.
codeExamples.title: Sorting records by a field

topics.theoryContent:
A lambda can take several parameters, separated by commas:

add = lambda a, b: a + b
print(add(3, 5))          # 8

full = lambda first, last: first + " " + last
print(full("Ravi", "Reddy"))

It can also take zero parameters, though that is rare:
say = lambda: "hello"

Real usage with more than one parameter is common in sorting complex data — for example sorting employee records by salary, where the lambda receives one item but reads several fields from it:

employees = [("Ravi", 50000), ("Anita", 90000)]
print(sorted(employees, key=lambda e: e[1]))   # by salary
topics.title: Lambda with multiple parameters

codeExamples.explanation: Multi-branch logic reads better as a named function than a squeezed lambda.
codeExamples.title: Same logic, named function

topics.theoryContent:
Lambdas are convenient, but they are not always the right tool. Three rules keep you out of trouble:

USE a lambda when:
- The logic is a single short expression.
- The function is used in exactly one place (like a sort key).

USE a named def when:
- The logic is more than one line.
- The function is used in several places — a name documents it and avoids repetition.
- The logic is complex enough that a name helps reading (and testing).

if/else inside a lambda is possible but ugly:
lambda x: "adult" if x >= 18 else "minor"

Beyond one expression, a def is clearer. Professionals treat lambdas as a convenience, not a goal — the rule is readability, not cleverness.
topics.title: Lambda vs named function

days.description: Today we are learning map, filter, and reduce.
days.title: map, filter, and reduce

topics.theoryContent:
Day 14 taught list comprehensions — Python's preferred way to build new lists. The functional tools map, filter and reduce solve the same families of problems through functions:

- map(f, list) — apply f to EVERY item, producing new values.
- filter(f, list) — keep only items where f(item) is True.
- reduce(f, list) — combine all items into ONE value.

These three cover the classic data pipeline: transform, select, aggregate. They come from functional programming, and Python ships them as built-ins (reduce lives in the functools module).

You already have a tool for most of this (comprehensions). map and filter are worth knowing because you will meet them in other people's code and in pandas-style data work — and they compose into one-line pipelines.
topics.title: The functional toolbox

codeExamples.code:
prices = [100, 250, 400]
display = list(map(lambda p: f"Rs {p}", prices))
print(display)
codeExamples.explanation: map applies the lambda to every price; list() materialises the results.
codeExamples.title: Formatting prices

topics.theoryContent:
map(f, collection) applies f to each item and returns an iterator of the results:

def double(x):
    return x * 2

nums = [1, 2, 3]
result = map(double, nums)
print(list(result))     # [2, 4, 6]

map returns a lazy iterator — it computes results on demand, so you pass it to list() to materialise it.

With a lambda it becomes a one-liner:
result = list(map(lambda x: x * 2, nums))

The same job with a comprehension:
result = [x * 2 for x in nums]

When you already have a named function, map reads well; otherwise the comprehension is usually clearer. Both are legitimate — the choice is readability.
topics.title: map — transform every item

codeExamples.code:
amounts = [0, 450, -20, 1200, 75]
valid = list(filter(lambda a: a > 0, amounts))
print(valid)
codeExamples.explanation: Only positive amounts pass the lambda test; zero and negative orders are dropped.
codeExamples.title: Filtering valid orders

topics.theoryContent:
filter(f, collection) keeps only the items for which f(item) is True:

def is_even(n):
    return n % 2 == 0

nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
evens = list(filter(is_even, nums))
print(evens)     # [2, 4, 6]

With a lambda:
evens = list(filter(lambda n: n % 2 == 0, nums))

The comprehension version:
evens = [n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]

filter KEEPS items where the function returns True — the function is the test, not the transform. This is the key mental model: map changes values, filter chooses which values survive.
topics.title: filter — keep the items that pass

codeExamples.code:
from functools import reduce
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
product = reduce(lambda a, b: a * b, nums)
print(product)
codeExamples.explanation: Each step multiplies the running total by the next item — a fold with a custom rule.
codeExamples.title: Product of all items

topics.theoryContent:
reduce(f, collection) combines the items one pair at a time until one value remains:

from functools import reduce

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

print(reduce(add, [1, 2, 3, 4]))    # 10

Trace it: add(1, 2) = 3, then add(3, 3) = 6, then add(6, 4) = 10. Each step folds the running result with the next item.

reduce lives in functools, so it needs an import. The built-in sum() already covers adding, and most reduce jobs have a simpler built-in:

- sum() instead of reduce(add, ...)
- max() / min() instead of the equivalent reduce

Use reduce when the combination is genuinely custom — building a product, concatenating with a rule, flattening nested structures. Otherwise prefer the built-in.
topics.title: reduce — fold a list into one value

codeExamples.code:
orders = [120, 0, 300, 45, 1000]
taxed = sum(p * 1.18 for p in orders if p > 0)
print(round(taxed, 2))
codeExamples.explanation: The generator expression filters, transforms and sums in one pass — the comprehension-style pipeline.
codeExamples.title: A one-line pipeline

topics.theoryContent:
The real power is chaining the tools: filter first, then map, then reduce.

orders = [120, 0, 300, 45, 1000]
taxed_total = reduce(
    lambda a, b: a + b,
    map(lambda p: p * 1.18,
        filter(lambda p: p > 0, orders))
)

Read it right to left: keep positive orders, apply 18% tax to each, then total them. Each stage feeds the next.

Python's comprehensions can express the same pipeline, and many programmers find them more readable:
taxed_total = sum(p * 1.18 for p in orders if p > 0)

There is no universal winner — pipelines shine when stages are named functions; comprehensions win for short inline logic. Know both, use the clearer one.
topics.title: Composing pipelines

codeExamples.explanation: With a named function, map reads cleanly — the function name documents the stage.
codeExamples.title: Named function with map

topics.theoryContent:
Both toolkits do the same work. Rules of thumb:

PREFER map/filter when:
- You already have a named function to apply: map(clean, rows).
- You want a lazy iterator without building a list.
- You are writing in a functional style with other named stages.

PREFER comprehensions when:
- The logic is a short expression you would have to wrap in a lambda.
- You need an if filter AND a transform together (comprehensions read naturally).
- You want a list/set/dict directly.

Modern Python style leans to comprehensions for most inline work, and map/filter when a real function already exists. Either is fine — the one the next reader understands faster is the one to ship.
topics.title: map/filter vs comprehensions — how to choose

workedExample.caseStudy: A server writes a log file that grows to gigabytes. The support team needs the count of ERROR lines and the first 3 error messages. Loading the whole file into a list is impossible; the analysis must stream the file one line at a time with a generator.
workedExample.code:
# Streaming log analysis
def read_lines(filename):
    with open(filename, "r") as file:
        for line in file:
            yield line

log = read_lines("server.log")
errors = (line for line in log if "ERROR" in line)

count = 0
first_three = []
for line in errors:
    count += 1
    if len(first_three) < 3:
        first_three.append(line.strip())

print("Total ERROR lines:", count)
print("First errors:")
for e in first_three:
    print(" ", e)
workedExample.codeExplanation: read_lines is a generator — the file is opened once and each line is yielded on demand, so a multi-gigabyte log never occupies memory. The generator expression errors() filters that stream for ERROR lines lazily. One pass consumes the stream, counting every match while keeping only the first three messages. This pattern — stream, filter, aggregate — is how real systems handle data too large to hold.

nums = iter([10, 20, 30])
print(next(nums))
print(next(nums))

codeExamples.explanation: iter() gets an iterator; next() pulls values one at a time until the collection ends.
codeExamples.title: Iterating manually

topics.theoryContent:
You have iterated for 20 days: for n in range(5), for name in names, for line in file. An ITERATOR is the machinery behind that — an object that hands you one value at a time on request.

The protocol is two methods:
- __iter__() — returns the iterator itself.
- __next__() — returns the next value, raising StopIteration when exhausted.

You rarely call these directly; the for loop does. But the idea matters: the for loop asks for one value, uses it, asks for the next. It never loads the whole collection into memory at once.

ITERABLE means "can be iterated" — lists, strings, tuples, dicts, sets, ranges, files, generators. When you write for x in something, that something is an iterable.
topics.title: What is an iterator?

codeExamples.explanation: The function pauses at each yield and resumes on the next demand — 1, 2, 3.
codeExamples.title: A generator in action

topics.title: Generators — functions that yield

codeExamples.explanation: Each line is produced and discarded one at a time — the file never loads into memory.
codeExamples.title: Line counts without loading the file

topics.theoryContent:
The payoff is memory. A list holds every value at once; a generator produces them on demand.

Squares of the first million numbers as a list:
squares = [n * n for n in range(1000000)]   # ~36 MB of ints at once

As a generator:
def squares(n):
    for i in range(n):
        yield i * i

for s in squares(1000000):
    pass     # only one number exists at a time

The list builds a million integers before anything can be used. The generator builds one, hands it out, discards it, builds the next. For huge or endless data, the generator is the only option that works at all.

Real use: processing a 10 GB log file line by line (Day 17 did this with for line in file — files are iterators), generating report rows, paging through API results.
topics.title: Why generators matter: memory

codeExamples.code:
total = sum(n * n for n in range(1_000_000))
print(total)
codeExamples.explanation: The generator expression feeds sum one value at a time — no million-item list is ever built.
codeExamples.title: Sum of a million squares

topics.theoryContent:
Comprehensions have a generator sibling: parentheses instead of square brackets.

List comprehension — builds the whole list:
squares = [n * n for n in range(10)]

Generator expression — lazy, produces on demand:
squares = (n * n for n in range(10))

You can loop over it or pass it to a function that accepts iterables:
total = sum(n * n for n in range(10))     # sum consumes it

The parentheses version is memory-efficient for large ranges, and many built-ins (sum, max, min, any, all) accept it directly.

Rule: if you only need to iterate once and the data may be large, a generator expression saves memory; if you need the values repeatedly or by index, keep the list.
topics.title: Generator expressions

codeExamples.code:
def ids():
    n = 1000
    while True:
        yield n
        n += 1

gen = ids()
print(next(gen))
print(next(gen))
print(next(gen))
codeExamples.explanation: Each next() pulls the next ID; the generator keeps its state between calls.
codeExamples.title: A never-ending ID counter

topics.theoryContent:
Because generators are lazy, they can represent sequences that never end — they produce the next value only when asked:

def evens():
    n = 0
    while True:
        yield n
        n += 2

gen = evens()
for _ in range(5):
    print(next(gen))     # 0 2 4 6 8

The while True inside is safe because the generator PAUSES at yield — it does not spin forever; it sleeps until the next value is requested.

This is impossible with a list — you cannot build an infinite list. Generators can. Real use: an ID counter that never repeats, a stream of readings, a lazy pagination that fetches the next page only when asked.
topics.title: Infinite sequences, safely

codeExamples.code:
import re
print(re.findall(r"S\w+", "Sita and Ravi saw Sam"))
codeExamples.explanation: S followed by word characters matches Sita and Sam but not Ravi.
codeExamples.title: Matching words that start with S

topics.theoryContent:
A REGULAR EXPRESSION (regex) is a compact pattern language for finding and manipulating text. Day 7 searched with in, find and count — but those find only exact strings. Regex matches PATTERNS: "a phone number", "an email", "any word starting with S".

The pattern is a string, and the re module applies it:

import re
pattern = r"S\w+"
text = "Sita and Ravi"
print(re.findall(pattern, text))    # ['Sita']

The r before the string makes it a RAW string — backslashes are passed through instead of being treated as escapes. Use r"" for every regex pattern.

Regex is the tool behind form validation (emails, phones, PAN numbers), log parsing, search-and-replace in editors, and most text-heavy systems. It is worth learning once — it repays the effort for a lifetime.
topics.title: What are regular expressions?

codeExamples.code:
import re
text = "Order 1001 shipped, order 2002 pending"
print(re.findall(r"\d+", text))
codeExamples.explanation: \d+ matches one or more digits anywhere in the text.
codeExamples.title: Finding numbers in text

topics.theoryContent:
Two functions cover most needs:

re.search(pattern, text) — find the FIRST match, or None.
re.findall(pattern, text) — find ALL matches as a list.

import re
text = "Order 1001 and order 2002"
m = re.search(r"\d+", text)
if m:
    print(m.group())      # 1001 — the matched text

print(re.findall(r"\d+", text))    # ['1001', '2002']

- search returns a match object (or None — always check it). m.group() is the matched text.
- findall returns the plain list of matches, ideal for scanning.

A common mistake: forgetting search returns None when there is no match, then calling .group() on None. Check first, like the example.
topics.title: re.search and re.findall

codeExamples.code:
import re
word = "programming"
print(re.findall(r"[aeiou]", word))
codeExamples.explanation: The character class matches every vowel — [o, a, i]
codeExamples.title: Extracting vowels

topics.theoryContent:
The pattern language is built from METACHARACTERS — symbols with special meaning:

.        any character except newline
\d       a digit (0-9)
\w       a word character (letter, digit, underscore)
\s       a whitespace character (space, tab, newline)
\D, \W, \S   the opposites

CHARACTER CLASSES match one of a set, written in square brackets:
[aeiou]     any vowel
[0-9]       any digit (same as \d)
[A-Z]       any uppercase letter
[a-z0-9]    any lowercase letter or digit
[^0-9]      NOT a digit (the ^ negates inside brackets)

phone = "Contact: 98765 43210"
print(re.findall(r"\d{5}", phone))     # 5-digit runs

Quantifiers like {5} say "exactly five" — more on those next.
topics.title: Metacharacters and character classes

codeExamples.code:
import re
text = "Support: 123-456-7890"
print(re.findall(r"\d{3}-\d{3}-\d{4}", text))
codeExamples.explanation: Three digit groups joined by hyphens, exactly as formatted phone numbers appear.
codeExamples.title: Matching a formatted number

topics.theoryContent:
ANCHORS pin the pattern to a position:
^    start of the string
$    end of the string

print(re.search(r"^Python", "Python is easy"))    # match
print(re.search(r"^Python", "I love Python"))     # None

QUANTIFIERS say how many times the previous thing may repeat:
*     zero or more
+     one or more
?     zero or one
{n}   exactly n
{n,}  n or more
{n,m} between n and m

phone = "Call 9876543210 now"
print(re.findall(r"\d{10}", phone))     # a 10-digit number

Combine them: r"\d{3}-\d{3}-\d{4}" matches a formatted US-style phone. Building patterns from these pieces is the whole skill.
topics.title: Anchors and quantifiers

codeExamples.code:
import re
text = "Pay Rs 500 and Rs 1200"
print(re.sub(r"Rs (\d+)", r"INR \1", text))
codeExamples.explanation: Each Rs <number> becomes INR <same number>, preserving the captured digits.
codeExamples.title: Swapping the currency label

topics.theoryContent:
GROUPS capture part of a match with round brackets:

import re
email = "ravi@college.edu.in"
m = re.search(r"(\w+)@(\w+[.\w]*)", email)
print(m.group(1))     # ravi — the username
print(m.group(2))     # college.edu.in — the domain

group(0) is the whole match; group(1), group(2) are the captured parts. Groups are how you EXTRACT structured pieces from matched text.

re.sub(pattern, replacement, text) replaces matches:
text = "Pay Rs 500 and Rs 1200"
print(re.sub(r"Rs (\d+)", r"INR \1", text))
# Pay INR 500 and INR 1200

In the replacement, \1 refers to the first group's text — the number is kept while the label changes. This is the regex version of replace() with patterns.
topics.title: Groups and re.sub

codeExamples.code:
import re
email = input("Enter email: ")
pattern = r"\w+@\w+\.[a-z]{2,}"
if re.search(pattern, email):
    print("Valid format")
else:
    print("Invalid format")
codeExamples.explanation: The pattern checks the classic username@domain.tld shape.
codeExamples.title: Validating a simple email

topics.theoryContent:
Patterns you will meet in real systems — save these as reference:

EMAIL — username@domain:
r"\w+@\w+\.[a-z]{2,}"

PHONE (Indian, 10 digits, optional +91):
r"\+?91?[-\s]?\d{10}"

PINCODE — six digits:
r"\b\d{6}\b"

WORD — with boundaries:
r"\bPython\b"     # the \b matches word boundaries

DATE — YYYY-MM-DD:
r"\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}"

None of these are perfect for every edge case — real email validation is famously hard — but they are the professional starting point. Test patterns on sample data before trusting them, and keep them raw strings with r"".
topics.title: Real-world patterns

codeExamples.code:
import json
data = {"name": "Ravi", "age": 21, "passed": True}
text = json.dumps(data)
print(text)
print(type(text))
codeExamples.explanation: dumps converts the Python dict into a JSON string.
codeExamples.title: JSON is text, Python is objects

topics.theoryContent:
JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the standard format for exchanging data between systems. It is just text with a strict structure:

{
  "name": "Ravi",
  "age": 21,
  "subjects": ["Python", "DBMS"],
  "passed": true
}

It looks exactly like a Python dictionary — that is deliberate. JSON supports four containers: objects ({...} — like dicts), arrays ([...] — like lists), and two scalar kinds: strings (in double quotes) and numbers. Booleans are true/false and null means "no value".

Why it matters: when your Python program talks to a website API, a database, or another company's system, the data almost always travels as JSON. Python's json module converts between JSON text and Python objects — the whole bridge.
topics.title: What is JSON?

codeExamples.explanation: indent=2 lays the JSON out for human reading, handy in reports and files.
codeExamples.title: Pretty-printed JSON

topics.theoryContent:
json.dumps converts a Python object into a JSON string:

import json
student = {"name": "Ravi", "age": 21, "marks": [70, 80]}
text = json.dumps(student)
print(text)     # {"name": "Ravi", "age": 21, "marks": [70, 80]}

The mapping is automatic:
- dict → JSON object
- list / tuple → JSON array
- str → JSON string
- int / float → JSON number
- True/False/None → true/false/null

Useful options:
json.dumps(student, indent=2)     # pretty, multi-line
json.dumps(student, sort_keys=True)   # alphabetical keys

If the data contains a set or a datetime, dumps fails — JSON has no direct equivalent. Convert first, or provide a default handler.
topics.title: json.dumps — Python to JSON

codeExamples.code:
import json
text = '{"name": "Ravi", "age": 21}'
student = json.loads(text)
print(student["name"])
print(student["age"])
codeExamples.explanation: loads turns the JSON text into a real dict, readable with normal bracket access.
codeExamples.title: Parsing a JSON string

topics.theoryContent:
json.loads converts a JSON string back into Python objects:

import json
text = '{"name": "Ravi", "age": 21}'
student = json.loads(text)
print(student["name"])     # Ravi

The round trip is symmetrical: dumps Python→JSON, loads JSON→Python.

Real data arrives as a JSON string — from an API response, a file, a webhook. The first thing a program does is loads it, then walks the resulting dicts and lists normally.

Broken JSON raises json.JSONDecodeError. Wrap loads in try/except when the source is untrusted — a malformed payload should be handled, not crash the program.
topics.title: json.loads — JSON to Python

codeExamples.code:
import json
data = {"name": "Ravi", "age": 21}
with open("student.json", "w") as file:
    json.dump(data, file, indent=2)

with open("student.json", "r") as file:
    loaded = json.load(file)
print(loaded)
codeExamples.explanation: dump writes the dict to the file; load reads it back as a dict — data survives between runs.
codeExamples.title: Persisting a record

topics.theoryContent:
JSON files are the simplest persistent data store you can build. The pattern matches Day 17 file handling, with json.load and json.dump (no trailing s — these work on files, not strings):

SAVING:
import json
data = {"name": "Ravi", "age": 21}
with open("student.json", "w") as file:
    json.dump(data, file, indent=2)

LOADING:
with open("student.json", "r") as file:
    data = json.load(file)
print(data["name"])

Memory hook:
- dumps/loads — strings.
- dump/load — files.

This is how small real systems persist data: read the JSON file at startup, work with the dicts in memory, write the file back when something changes. It is the poor-man's database — and for many tools it is enough.
topics.title: Reading and writing JSON files

codeExamples.explanation: The loop walks the students array; each student's marks array is averaged.
codeExamples.title: Walking nested JSON

topics.title: Nested JSON

codeExamples.code:
import json
text = '{"name": "Ravi"}'
data = json.loads(text)
age = data.get("age", "unknown")
print(data["name"], age)
codeExamples.explanation: .get() returns a default when "age" is absent — optional fields never crash the program.
codeExamples.title: Safe parsing of optional fields

topics.theoryContent:
Handling bad JSON is part of working with real data:

import json
try:
    data = json.loads('{"name": "Ravi"')     # missing closing brace
except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
    print("Bad JSON:", e)

Key facts:
- A missing key still raises KeyError — use .get() for optional fields.
- Missing values are often null in JSON, arriving as Python None.
- Large JSON loads into memory at once; for huge files you would stream with json.JSONDecoder per line (Day 23-style).

Treat every payload from the outside as suspect: wrap loads in try/except, use .get() for optional fields, and validate before trusting. That habit prevents a whole class of crashes.
topics.title: JSON errors and safety

days.title: Working with CSV Files

codeExamples.code:
name,age
Ravi,21
Anita,22
codeExamples.explanation: Header row plus data rows — the structure your spreadsheet exports and imports.
codeExamples.title: CSV is a plain-text table

topics.theoryContent:
CSV (Comma-Separated Values) is the plain-text table format used everywhere: spreadsheets export it, banks send statements in it, data analysts exchange it.

name,age,branch
Ravi,21,CSE
Anita,22,ECE

Rules are simple:
- One ROW per line.
- FIELDS separated by commas.
- The first row often holds the HEADERS (column names).

Day 7 parsed a CSV line by hand with split(","). That works for clean data — but real CSV has traps: fields containing commas ("Reddy, Ravi"), quotes, blank lines, newlines inside fields. The csv module handles all of it correctly. Always use it instead of hand-splitting.
topics.title: What is CSV?

codeExamples.code:
import csv
with open("students.csv", "r") as file:
    reader = csv.reader(file)
    header = next(reader)
    for row in reader:
        print(row[0], "age", row[1])
codeExamples.explanation: next() takes the header; the loop prints each data row's fields by index.
codeExamples.title: Reading a CSV file

topics.theoryContent:
csv.reader reads a file and hands back each row as a list of fields:

import csv
with open("students.csv", "r") as file:
    reader = csv.reader(file)
    for row in reader:
        print(row)

Each row is a list — ['Ravi', '21', 'CSE'].

reader handles all the CSV pitfalls automatically: commas inside quoted fields, quoted fields with newlines, and inconsistent line endings.

Common processing:
with open("students.csv", "r") as file:
    reader = csv.reader(file)
    header = next(reader)          # the first row
    for row in reader:             # the data rows
        print(row)

next(reader) skips the header so the loop sees only data. Remember every field is a STRING — convert numbers before arithmetic.
topics.title: csv.reader — reading rows

codeExamples.code:
import csv
with open("students.csv", "r") as file:
    for row in csv.DictReader(file):
        print(f"{row['name']} in {row['branch']}")
codeExamples.explanation: Each row is a dict keyed by the header names — no index juggling.
codeExamples.title: Reading with DictReader

topics.theoryContent:
DictReader uses the header row as keys, so every row becomes a dictionary:

import csv
with open("students.csv", "r") as file:
    reader = csv.DictReader(file)
    for row in reader:
        print(row["name"], row["age"], row["branch"])

Rows are now readable by name instead of index: row["name"] instead of row[0]. If the file has no header, pass the fieldnames yourself:
reader = csv.DictReader(file, fieldnames=["name", "age", "branch"])

DictReader is the professional default — named fields make the code self-documenting and immune to column reordering.
topics.title: csv.DictReader — rows as dictionaries

codeExamples.code:
import csv
with open("out.csv", "w", newline="") as file:
    writer = csv.writer(file)
    writer.writerow(["name", "age"])
    writer.writerow(["Ravi", 21])
    writer.writerow(["Anita", 22])
codeExamples.explanation: The header and two data rows are written; commas in any field would be quoted automatically.
codeExamples.title: Writing a CSV

topics.theoryContent:
csv.writer writes lists of fields as correctly formatted rows:

import csv
with open("out.csv", "w", newline="") as file:
    writer = csv.writer(file)
    writer.writerow(["name", "age"])        # one row
    writer.writerow(["Ravi", 21])
    writer.writerow(["Anita", 22])

- writerow(row) writes one row; writerows(rows) writes many at once.
- The newline="" argument matters on Windows — without it, blank lines appear between rows.

writer handles the tricky cases for you: fields with commas get quoted automatically, so "Reddy, Ravi" survives the round trip intact.
topics.title: csv.writer — writing rows

codeExamples.code:
import csv
rows = [{"name": "Ravi", "age": 21}, {"name": "Anita", "age": 22}]
with open("out.csv", "w", newline="") as file:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(file, fieldnames=["name", "age"])
    writer.writeheader()
    writer.writerows(rows)
codeExamples.explanation: fieldnames sets the columns, writeheader writes them, writerows dumps the record list.
codeExamples.title: Writing dicts to CSV

topics.theoryContent:
DictWriter pairs with DictReader: it writes dicts using a declared field order.

import csv
with open("out.csv", "w", newline="") as file:
    fieldnames = ["name", "age", "branch"]
    writer = csv.DictWriter(file, fieldnames=fieldnames)
    writer.writeheader()
    writer.writerow({"name": "Ravi", "age": 21, "branch": "CSE"})

- fieldnames declares the column order.
- writeheader() writes the header row from fieldnames.
- writerow(dict) writes one record.

If a dict is missing a field, the cell is empty; if it has an extra field, DictWriter raises ValueError. The round trip — DictReader in, DictWriter out — is how real pipelines migrate, filter, and enrich tabular data.
topics.title: DictWriter — writing dictionaries

topics.theoryContent:
Almost every real system cares about when things happened: orders have order dates, payments have timestamps, memberships have expiry dates. The datetime module is the standard way to work with dates and times.

Its main pieces:
- datetime.date — a calendar date (year, month, day).
- datetime.time — a time of day (hour, minute, second).
- datetime.datetime — date AND time together.
- datetime.timedelta — a span of time (5 days, 2 hours).
- datetime.today() — right now.

import datetime
today = datetime.date.today()
print(today)                    # 2026-08-12
print(today.year, today.month)  # 2026 8

Dates are first-class objects: they know their parts, they compare, and they do arithmetic. That is far safer than treating dates as strings.

topics.theoryContent:
Build specific dates by passing year, month, day:

import datetime
d = datetime.date(2026, 8, 15)
print(d)                # 2026-08-15

And full datetimes:
now = datetime.datetime(2026, 8, 12, 10, 30, 0)
print(now)              # 2026-08-12 10:30:00

A date object answers questions about itself:
d = datetime.date(2026, 8, 15)
print(d.weekday())      # 5 — Monday=0, so Saturday
print(d.day, d.month, d.year)

Comparing dates works naturally:
if d > datetime.date.today():
    print("Future date")

topics.theoryContent:
A date object is great for logic, but users want "15 Aug 2026", not "2026-08-15". strftime (string-format-time) converts a date to any text format using codes:

import datetime
d = datetime.date(2026, 8, 15)

print(d.strftime("%d/%m/%Y"))     # 15/08/2026
print(d.strftime("%B %d, %Y"))    # August 15, 2026
print(d.strftime("%A"))           # Saturday

The most useful codes:
%d  day (01-31)      %m  month (01-12)      %Y  year (2026)
%b  month short (Aug)   %B  month full (August)
%A  weekday (Saturday)  %a  weekday short (Sat)
%H  hour 24h (14)    %M  minute             %S  second

Every report, invoice and notification formats dates with strftime — it is the output formatter for time.
topics.title: strftime — formatting dates for humans

codeExamples.code:

topics.theoryContent:
The reverse of strftime: strptime (string-parse-time) reads a date from text using the same codes. This is how dates arrive from files, forms and APIs:

import datetime
text = "15/08/2026"
d = datetime.datetime.strptime(text, "%d/%m/%Y")
print(d.date())      # 2026-08-15

The format string must match the text EXACTLY — "%d/%m/%Y" will not parse "2026-08-15". This is the most common source of bugs: mismatch between the actual text and the format.

A wrong format raises ValueError, so real programs parse inside try/except. Dates from CSV files, API responses and web forms are all strptime territory.
topics.title: strptime — parsing dates from text

topics.theoryContent:
timedelta represents a span of time and lets you do date arithmetic:

import datetime
today = datetime.date.today()
due = today + datetime.timedelta(days=30)
print(due)               # 30 days from today

You can add, subtract, and multiply deltas:
- datetime.timedelta(days=30, hours=5, minutes=10)
- today - datetime.timedelta(weeks=2)   # two weeks ago
- Subtracting two dates gives a timedelta.

days_left = due - today
print(days_left.days)    # 30

Real uses: membership expiry (issue date + 1 year), overdue detection (due date < today), reminders (event date - 3 days), and calculating ages and tenure.
