codeExamples.code:
def countdown(n):
    if n <= 0:            # base case
        print("Blast off!")
        return
    print(n)
    countdown(n - 1)      # recursive case — smaller problem

countdown(3)
codeExamples.explanation: Each call prints n and calls itself with n-1, until the base case stops the chain.
codeExamples.title: Counting down recursively

topics.theoryContent:
RECURSION is when a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem. It is the natural way to describe structures that contain themselves: folders inside folders, branches inside branches, "n factorial" defined in terms of "(n-1) factorial".

Every recursive function has two parts:

1. BASE CASE — the smallest problem, answered directly, where the recursion STOPS.
2. RECURSIVE CASE — the step that calls the function with a smaller input.

Without a base case, recursion never stops and Python raises RecursionError. The base case is the exit — like the loop condition in Day 6.
topics.title: What is recursion?

codeExamples.explanation: n <= 1 is the base case; otherwise the function multiplies n by the factorial of n-1.
codeExamples.title: Factorial recursively

topics.theoryContent:
The factorial of n (n!) is n × (n-1) × ... × 1. Its definition is naturally recursive:
- 0! = 1                     (base case)
- n! = n × (n-1)!            (recursive case)

def factorial(n):
    if n <= 1:
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)

Trace factorial(4):
factorial(4) = 4 * factorial(3)
             = 4 * (3 * factorial(2))
             = 4 * (3 * (2 * factorial(1)))
             = 4 * (3 * (2 * 1))
             = 24

The calls stack up, each waiting for the one below, then unwind from the base case back up. This "defer, then return" behaviour is the shape of every recursion.
topics.title: Factorial — the classic example

codeExamples.explanation: First element plus the recursive sum of the tail, ending at the empty-list base case.
codeExamples.title: Sum with recursion

topics.theoryContent:
Recursion handles collections too. The sum of a list is: the first element plus the sum of the rest — a smaller list. Eventually the rest is empty and the sum is 0 (the base case).

def recursive_sum(nums):
    if not nums:              # base case — empty list
        return 0
    return nums[0] + recursive_sum(nums[1:])

print(recursive_sum([1, 2, 3, 4]))    # 10

Each call slices off the first element and recurses on the remainder. This version is deliberately simple to teach recursion — in practice you would use sum(), but the SHAPE is what matters: shrinking the problem until it hits a base case.

The list-slice version is also wasteful (each slice copies). A cleaner real version keeps an index, but the idea is identical.
topics.title: Summing a list recursively

codeExamples.explanation: The loop wins on simplicity for flat lists; recursion shines on nested structures.
codeExamples.title: Same job, loop vs recursion

topics.theoryContent:
Everything recursive can be written with a loop — and sometimes the loop is better.

PREFER recursion when the problem itself is nested or self-similar:
- Directory trees (folders within folders).
- File systems.
- Nested data structures.
- Divide-and-conquer algorithms (sorting, searching — Days 29-30).

PREFER loops when the problem is a simple count or accumulation:
- Summing, counting, stepping — a for/while loop is clearer.
- Deep recursion has a cost: each call uses stack memory, and Python limits recursion depth (~1000). A loop over 100,000 items is fine; a recursion over them crashes.

Rule of thumb: if the structure you walk is naturally nested, recurse; if it is a flat sequence, loop.
topics.title: Recursion vs loops

codeExamples.explanation: Folders recurse, files add one — the nesting depth is handled automatically.
codeExamples.title: Counting files in nested folders

topics.theoryContent:
Recursion's real home is data nested to unknown depth — like a file system or a nested comment tree:

def count_files(folder):
    total = 0
    for item in folder:
        if isinstance(item, list):     # a sub-folder
            total += count_files(item)
        else:                          # a file name
            total += 1
    return total

tree = ["report.pdf", ["docs", ["python.txt", "data.csv"]], "notes.md"]
print(count_files(tree))     # 4 files

The function cannot know how deep the nesting goes — it just handles "item is a file" (base) and "item is a folder" (recurse). This self-similar handling of arbitrary depth is impossible to write cleanly with a plain loop, and it is the reason recursion exists.
topics.title: Recursion on nested structures

days.title: Sorting Algorithms

topics.theoryContent:
Day 8 used sorted() without thinking about how it works. Sorting is the most-studied problem in computer science because it teaches the core ideas: comparing, swapping, nested loops, and — most importantly — that the SAME task can be done in wildly different amounts of work.

The built-in sorted() is excellent and you should use it in real code. But learning the classic algorithms teaches you to THINK like an algorithm designer:
- How to measure work (how many comparisons?).
- How loops interact.
- When a naive approach is fine and when it is not.

Today you implement three classic sorts with plain loops. None of them beat sorted() in practice — the lesson is the mechanics, not the final answer.
topics.title: Why study sorting?

codeExamples.explanation: Adjacent swaps push the largest unsorted value to the end on every pass.
codeExamples.title: Bubble sort

topics.title: Bubble sort

codeExamples.explanation: Each pass locates the smallest remaining value and puts it in place.
codeExamples.title: Selection sort

topics.title: Selection sort

codeExamples.explanation: Each item is inserted into the sorted prefix by shifting larger items right.
codeExamples.title: Insertion sort

topics.theoryContent:
Insertion sort builds the sorted list one item at a time, inserting each new item into its correct place among the already-sorted ones — like a person sorting a hand of cards:

def insertion_sort(nums):
    for i in range(1, len(nums)):
        current = nums[i]
        j = i - 1
        while j >= 0 and nums[j] > current:
            nums[j + 1] = nums[j]
            j -= 1
        nums[j + 1] = current
    return nums

The while loop shifts larger items right to make room, then the current value drops into the gap.

Insertion sort is the fastest of the three on nearly-sorted data — it can run in near-linear time when few items are out of place. Real systems use this property: sorting a nearly-sorted stream with insertion sort is often the pragmatic choice.
topics.title: Insertion sort

codeExamples.code:
import random, time
nums = [random.randint(0, 100000) for _ in range(10000)]

start = time.time()
sorted(nums)
print("Built-in sorted:", round(time.time() - start, 4), "s")
codeExamples.explanation: The built-in sorts 10,000 items in milliseconds — vastly faster than the O(n²) classics.
codeExamples.title: Built-in wins on big data

topics.theoryContent:
All three are O(n²) on average — the same class of slowness. The differences:

BUBBLE — simplest to explain, most swaps. Only teaching value.
SELECTION — fewest swaps (n total). Good when swapping is costly; indifferent to input order.
INSERTION — best on nearly-sorted data (can be near O(n)). Best of the three for real use.

Work grows with the square of the size. Doubling the list quadruples the work:
- 1,000 items → ~1,000,000 steps.
- 10,000 items → ~100,000,000 steps.

For anything real, the built-in sorted() uses Timsort — an O(n log n) hybrid that beats all three dramatically on large data. The takeaway: know these algorithms to understand the craft, and reach for sorted() in production.
topics.title: Comparing the three

codeExamples.code:
people = [("A", 30), ("B", 20), ("C", 30)]
by_age = sorted(people, key=lambda p: p[1])
by_name_then_age = sorted(by_age, key=lambda p: p[0])
print(by_name_then_age)
codeExamples.explanation: Sort by age first, then by name; stable ties keep the age order inside equal names.
codeExamples.title: Two-key sorting with stability

topics.theoryContent:
Two built-in features are worth remembering:

KEY — sort by a derived value (Day 21 lambdas):
words = ["apple", "kiwi", "strawberry"]
print(sorted(words, key=len))        # shortest first

records = [("Ravi", 85), ("Anita", 92)]
print(sorted(records, key=lambda r: r[1]))   # by score

STABILITY — items that compare equal keep their original order:
people = [("A", 30), ("B", 20), ("C", 30)]
by_age = sorted(people, key=lambda p: p[1])
# A(30) before C(30) — original order preserved

Stability enables sorting by two keys: sort by the second key, then by the first. The second sort respects the first one's order within ties.
topics.title: Sorting with custom keys and stability

days.title: Searching Algorithms

topics.theoryContent:
Searching is the other half of the algorithm canon: given a collection, find whether a value is present (and where).

You already have two ways:
- in — "is it present?"
- list.index(value) — "where is it?"

Both do a LINEAR search under the hood: scan item by item from the start. That is fine for small lists and essential for unsorted data. But a sorted list opens a far faster door — binary search — which cuts the work dramatically the bigger the data gets.

The lesson of this day is the SAME as Day 29: use the built-ins in real code (they implement these algorithms in C), and study the mechanics to understand the difference in effort.
topics.title: The searching problem

codeExamples.explanation: enumerate supplies the index while the loop compares each value; -1 means not found.
codeExamples.title: Linear search

topics.theoryContent:
Linear search checks each item in order until it finds the target or reaches the end:

def linear_search(nums, target):
    for i, value in enumerate(nums):
        if value == target:
            return i
    return -1

print(linear_search([4, 2, 9, 1], 9))     # 2
print(linear_search([4, 2, 9, 1], 7))     # -1

- Works on ANY list, sorted or not.
- Best case: target at the start — one step.
- Worst case: target missing — every item checked, n steps.

Linear search is the fallback that always works. When the data has no order, it is the only option. When the data is huge, its cost (up to n checks) is the reason sorted data matters.
topics.title: Linear search

codeExamples.code:
data = [1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49]
print(len(data))
codeExamples.explanation: A sorted list is the precondition for binary search — order is what lets you discard half at every step.
codeExamples.title: Halving the search space

topics.theoryContent:
Binary search exploits a sorted list. Instead of checking items one by one, it compares the target against the MIDDLE item and halves the search space on every step:

Sorted:  [1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49]
Searching for 36:
1. Middle is 16. 36 > 16 → target is in the RIGHT half.
2. Right half: [25, 36, 49]. Middle is 36. Found it!

The key insight: because the list is sorted, comparing with the middle tells you which half to DISCARD. Every step throws away half the remaining items.

Work grows as log₂(n):
- 1,000 items → ~10 steps.
- 1,000,000 items → ~20 steps.
- 1,000,000,000 items → ~30 steps.

That is the payoff — from a million checks to twenty.
topics.title: Binary search — the idea

codeExamples.explanation: Each loop iteration halves the interval; low overrunning high means the target is absent.

codeExamples.explanation: The interval narrows to empty, low exceeds high, and the function reports -1.

topics.theoryContent:
Walk through binary_search([1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49], 36):

STEP 1: low=0, high=6, mid=(0+6)//2=3. nums[3]=16. 36 > 16 → low=4.
Search space: [25, 36, 49]

STEP 2: low=4, high=6, mid=5. nums[5]=36. Match → return 5.

Two steps for seven items. Try searching for 8:
STEP 1: mid=3, 16. 8 < 16 → high=2. Space: [1, 4, 9]
STEP 2: mid=1, 4. 8 > 4 → low=2. Space: [9]
STEP 3: mid=2, 9. 8 < 9 → high=1. Now low=2 > high=1 → return -1.

Notice high jumps BELOW mid (mid-1), because nums[mid] was already checked. The interval shrinks without skipping anything.
topics.title: Tracing binary search

print(pos, data[pos])
codeExamples.explanation: bisect_left returns the insertion point; if data[pos] equals the target, it is present.
codeExamples.title: Binary search via bisect

topics.theoryContent:
The standard library implements binary search in the bisect module. For sorted lists, bisect_left and bisect_right locate insertion points — and searching is a one-liner:

import bisect
data = [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]

pos = bisect.bisect_left(data, 16)
found = pos < len(data) and data[pos] == 16
print(found)     # True

For membership on sorted data:
if 16 in data:   # linear — fine for small lists

Real systems use bisect when they must keep a list sorted while inserting — inserting into a sorted list with insort stays faster than re-sorting. Like everything this day: understand the algorithm, then let the standard library do the heavy lifting.
topics.title: The bisect module — binary search built in

codeExamples.explanation: A dict finds a key in constant time — faster than any scan for repeated lookups.

topics.theoryContent:
Deciding between the approaches:

LINEAR SEARCH when:
- The list is small (a dozen items — the difference is irrelevant).
- The list is NOT sorted.
- You only need yes/no: use in.

BINARY SEARCH when:
- The list is large AND sorted.
- Speed matters (repeated lookups in a big dataset).
- The built-in bisect is always the right implementation.

For very large sorted data, a dictionary (Day 10) is even faster — instant lookups. The rule of thumb in real systems: if lookups dominate and the key set is fixed, use a dict; if you must keep a sorted list for range queries, use bisect.

topics.theoryContent:
Everything so far has been a one-dimensional list: a row of items. Python lets a list hold other lists, and that gives you a grid — a two-dimensional structure with rows and columns.

matrix = [
    [1, 2, 3],
    [4, 5, 6],
    [7, 8, 9],
]

The outer list is the rows. Each inner list is a row, and inside each row the positions are columns. To reach a value you give two indexes in order: matrix[row][col].

matrix[0]    → the first row: [1, 2, 3]
matrix[1][2] → row 1, column 2: 6

Indexing still starts at 0, for both rows and columns. The first index picks the row, the second picks the column inside that row.

topics.theoryContent:
With nested loops you can compute anything across a grid.

SUM OF A ROW:
def row_sum(grid, r):
    return sum(grid[r])

TOTAL OF THE GRID:
total = sum(sum(row) for row in grid)

LARGEST VALUE:
biggest = max(max(row) for row in grid)

TRANSPOSE (swap rows and columns):
transposed = [[grid[c][r] for c in range(len(grid))] for r in range(len(grid[0]))]

Each is a few lines, but each one hides real thought about which index is the row and which is the column. Getting rows and columns swapped is the single most common matrix bug.

topics.theoryContent:
Grids are everywhere once you look:

- A marksheet is rows of students and columns of subjects.
- A cinema or bus seat map is rows and columns of taken/free.
- A game like Tic-Tac-Toe, Chess, or Sudoku is a board of rows and columns.
- An image is a grid of pixels, each pixel a small list of red/green/blue values.
- A map or a maze is a grid of cells.

The pattern is always the same: model the real-world grid as a 2D list, then use nested loops to read or update it. Once a student can index grid[r][c] without hesitation, games, image code, and data tables all become approachable.

codeExamples.title: Passing a function to a function

topics.theoryContent:
A function is not magic — it is a value like a number or a string. You can store it, pass it to another function, and return it.

def greet(name):
    return f"Hello, {name}"

f = greet          # no () — we are passing the function itself
print(f("ravi"))   # Hello, ravi

Notice the difference: greet refers to the function, greet("ravi") calls it. The moment a function can be passed around like data, you can write functions ABOUT functions. Those are called higher-order functions, and they unlock the decorator.
topics.title: Functions are objects

codeExamples.code:
def loud(func):
    def wrapped(*args, **kwargs):
        print(">>> calling", func.__name__)
        result = func(*args, **kwargs)
        print("<<< done")
        return result
    return wrapped

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

add = loud(add)
print(add(3, 4))
codeExamples.explanation: *args, **kwargs let the wrapper accept any arguments the wrapped function takes.
codeExamples.title: A manual wrapper

topics.theoryContent:
A wrapper is a function that adds behaviour before and/or after another function.

def loud(func):
    def wrapped(*args, **kwargs):
        print(">>> calling", func.__name__)
        result = func(*args, **kwargs)
        print("<<< done")
        return result
    return wrapped

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

add = loud(add)          # replace add with its wrapped version
print(add(3, 4))

The loud function takes a function, builds a new function around it, and returns that new function. The original code that calls add never changes — it just gets a more talkative version. This is the decorator pattern, written by hand.
topics.title: Wrapping a function

topics.theoryContent:
The standard library (Days 25-30: json, csv, datetime, math...) covers a lot, but the real strength of Python is its community of packages — extra code anyone can install. Around 500,000 packages are published, and they cover nearly every need: data analysis (pandas), web servers (flask, django), machine learning (scikit-learn, tensorflow), and thousands more.

A package is just a collection of modules published so others can reuse them. Instead of writing an Excel reader from scratch, you pip install openpyxl and import it.

pip is Python's package installer. It downloads a package from the Python Package Index (PyPI) and installs it into your environment.

topics.theoryContent:
The core pip commands to memorise:

pip install requests          # install the latest version
pip install requests==2.31.0  # install a specific version
pip install --upgrade pip     # upgrade pip itself
pip uninstall requests        # remove it
pip list                      # what is installed
pip show requests             # details about one package

A version like 2.31.0 has three parts: major, minor, patch. Major bumps can break code, patch bumps usually cannot. Real projects pin versions so the same code works everywhere.

topics.theoryContent:
Different projects need different packages — and sometimes different VERSIONS of the same package. Project A needs pandas 1.5, project B needs pandas 2.1. Installing both globally causes conflicts.

A virtual environment is an isolated Python world per project: each project gets its own copy of Python's packages, so what you install in one never touches another.

python -m venv .venv        # create the environment (one time)
.venv\Scripts\activate      # Windows: turn it on
source .venv/bin/activate    # macOS/Linux: turn it on

While activated, pip installs go into this environment only. When you are done: deactivate.

When you install the packages a project needs, record them so anyone can rebuild the same environment:

pip freeze > requirements.txt

This writes every installed package with its exact version. To recreate the environment on a new machine — a teammate's laptop, a server, a friend's PC — run:

pip install -r requirements.txt

A requirements.txt is the contract that says "this project needs exactly these packages at these versions." Sharing a project without it leaves the next person guessing what to install, and guessing is how version conflicts start.

codeExamples.code:
import requests
resp = requests.get("https://api.example.com/weather", params={"city": "Mumbai"})
print(resp.status_code)
print(resp.json())
codeExamples.explanation: requests.get sends the request; .json() decodes the reply body into Python data.
codeExamples.title: The shape of an API call

topics.theoryContent:
An API (Application Programming Interface) is a doorway other programs provide so your program can use their data or services. A weather website does not want you scraping its HTML — it offers an API endpoint: a URL that returns clean data (usually JSON) when you ask.

The exchange uses HTTP, the same protocol browsers use. Your program sends a GET request to a URL; the server replies with a status code and a body:

GET https://api.example.com/weather?city=Mumbai

200 means OK. 404 means not found. 401/403 mean unauthorised — usually a missing or wrong API key.

The body of a successful reply is JSON (Day 25), which Python parses straight into dicts and lists. That is the whole trick: the web is just HTTP plus JSON.
topics.title: What an API is

codeExamples.code:
import requests
resp = requests.get("https://api.example.com/weather", params={"city": "Mumbai"})
if resp.status_code == 200:
    data = resp.json()
    print(data["temp"])
else:
    print(f"Request failed: {resp.status_code}")
codeExamples.explanation: The guard prevents crashing on an error body that has no "temp" key.
codeExamples.title: Checking before parsing

topics.theoryContent:
Never assume the request succeeded. The status code is the server's report card:

2xx — success (200 OK, 201 Created)
3xx — redirect (the server points elsewhere)
4xx — your fault (400 bad request, 401/403 no permission, 404 not found)
5xx — the server's fault (500 internal error, 503 service unavailable)

Good code checks before parsing:

resp = requests.get(url)
if resp.status_code == 200:
    data = resp.json()
else:
    print("Failed:", resp.status_code, resp.text)

Modern requests can even raise an exception for bad statuses via resp.raise_for_status(). Either way: check, then parse.
topics.title: Reading status codes

import os
import requests

key = os.environ.get("MY_API_KEY", "")
headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}"}
resp = requests.get(
    "https://api.example.com/data",
    headers=headers,
    params={"city": "Delhi", "limit": 5},
)
print(resp.json() if resp.status_code == 200 else resp.status_code)
codeExamples.explanation: The key never appears in the URL or in the code itself — it comes from the environment.
codeExamples.title: Using an API key from an environment variable

topics.theoryContent:
Real APIs usually ask for parameters in the URL — which city, how many results — and often an API key so they know who is calling and how to bill usage.

API keys are secrets. Never write them directly into code that will be shared. Standard practice is an environment variable:

import os
key = os.environ["MY_API_KEY"]

resp = requests.get(
    "https://api.example.com/data",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}"},
    params={"city": "Delhi", "units": "metric"},
)

The params dict becomes ?city=Delhi&units=metric in the URL. The key travels in the headers, out of the URL and out of your logs.
topics.title: Query parameters and API keys

resp = requests.get("https://api.exchangerate-api.com/v4/latest/USD", timeout=10)
if resp.status_code != 200:

topics.theoryContent:
Files (Day 17) are fine for a few records, but they fail at scale: reading a whole file to find one record, two programs editing it at once, no structure to enforce that a row is complete. A database fixes all three.

SQLite is a database stored as a single file — no server to run, no install beyond Python itself, the standard library has sqlite3. It speaks SQL (Structured Query Language), a decades-old language for storing and querying tables.

A table is a grid like a spreadsheet: columns have names and types, rows are records. The core operations are CRUD — Create, Read, Update, Delete — and SQL spells them INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE.

import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect("students.db")
cur = conn.cursor()
cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES (?, ?)", ("ravi", 87))
cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES (?, ?)", ("anita", 93))
conn.commit()

cur.execute("SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks >= 80")
for row in cur.fetchall():
    print(row)
conn.close()
codeExamples.explanation: The ? placeholders keep values out of the SQL string, preventing injection.

topics.theoryContent:
Writing and reading rows:

cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES (?, ?)", ("ravi", 87))

The ? are placeholders: the actual values are passed separately. Never build SQL by string concatenation — that is how SQL injection works (user input sneaking into your query).

SELECT retrieves rows; the WHERE clause filters them:

cur.execute("SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks >= 80")
for row in cur.fetchall():
    print(row)

fetchall returns a list of tuples. Each tuple is one row, columns in the order you listed them.
topics.title: INSERT and SELECT

codeExamples.code:
import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect("students.db")
cur = conn.cursor()
cur.execute("UPDATE students SET marks = 90 WHERE name = ?", ("ravi",))
cur.execute("DELETE FROM students WHERE marks < 40")
conn.commit()

cur.execute("SELECT name, marks FROM students")
for row in cur.fetchall():
    print(row)
conn.close()
codeExamples.explanation: Both statements name an exact WHERE; the transaction is saved with commit.
codeExamples.title: Update and delete safely

topics.theoryContent:
Changing and removing data needs a WHERE clause too — otherwise every row in the table changes.

cur.execute("UPDATE students SET marks = 90 WHERE name = ?", ("ravi",))
cur.execute("DELETE FROM students WHERE marks < 40", ())

The golden rule of UPDATE and DELETE: if you cannot picture exactly which rows the WHERE matches, do not run it. A missing WHERE on a DELETE removes the entire table — that is the classic database disaster. Run SELECT with the same WHERE first to preview.
topics.title: UPDATE and DELETE

codeExamples.code:
import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect("students.db")
cur = conn.cursor()
try:
    cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES (?, ?)", ("sita", 76))
    cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES (?, ?)", ("mohan", 95))
    conn.commit()
    print("Saved.")
except Exception as e:
    conn.rollback()
    print("Rolled back:", e)
conn.close()
codeExamples.explanation: commit makes both inserts permanent; any failure rolls the batch back entirely.
codeExamples.title: Transaction with rollback

topics.theoryContent:
A transaction is a batch of changes that must all succeed together. SQLite groups statements into a transaction; nothing is saved until you call commit.

If you close the connection without commit, the changes vanish. If something fails mid-batch, you can rollback to undo everything since the last commit:

try:
    cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES (?, ?)", (name, marks))
    cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES (?, ?)", (name2, marks2))
    conn.commit()
except Exception:
    conn.rollback()
    print("Changes undone")

Either both rows are saved or neither is. For anything where money or marks are involved, that atomicity is exactly what you want.
topics.title: Transactions: commit and rollback

json.dump cannot serialise objects directly. The trick: convert to a dict before saving and rebuild objects after loading.

def book_to_dict(book):

# Inventory and Billing System
import sqlite3
from datetime import date

def setup(conn):
    cur = conn.cursor()
    cur.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS products (
        id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL,
        price REAL NOT NULL, stock INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0)""")
    cur.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS sales (
        id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, product TEXT,
        qty INTEGER, total REAL, day TEXT)""")
    conn.commit()

def add_product(cur, name, price, stock):
    cur.execute("INSERT INTO products (name, price, stock) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
                (name, price, stock))
    conn.commit()
    print("Product added.")

def list_inventory(cur):
    cur.execute("SELECT name, price, stock FROM products")
    for name, price, stock in cur.fetchall():
        flag = "  <-- LOW" if stock < 5 else ""
        print(f"{name}: Rs {price} x {stock}{flag}")

def make_sale(cur, name, qty):
    cur.execute("SELECT price, stock FROM products WHERE name = ?", (name,))
    row = cur.fetchone()
    if not row or row[1] < qty:
        print("Not enough stock or unknown product.")
        return
    price, stock = row
    cur.execute("UPDATE products SET stock = stock - ? WHERE name = ?", (qty, name))
    cur.execute("INSERT INTO sales (product, qty, total, day) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)",
                (name, qty, price * qty, str(date.today())))
    print("=" * 30)
    print(f"{name} x {qty}  = Rs {price * qty:.2f}")
    print("Thank you, visit again!")
    print("=" * 30)

def daily_total(cur):
    cur.execute("SELECT SUM(total) FROM sales WHERE day = ?", (str(date.today()),))
    print(f"Today's sales: Rs {cur.fetchone()[0] or 0:.2f}")

conn = sqlite3.connect("shop.db")
setup(conn)
cur = conn.cursor()
while True:
    print("\n1 Add product  2 Inventory  3 Sale  4 Daily total  5 Exit")
    choice = input("Choose: ").strip()
    if choice == "1":
        add_product(cur, input("Name: "), float(input("Price: ")), int(input("Stock: ")))
    elif choice == "2":
        list_inventory(cur)
    elif choice == "3":
        make_sale(cur, input("Product: "), int(input("Qty: ")))
        conn.commit()
    elif choice == "4":
        daily_total(cur)
    elif choice == "5":
        conn.commit()
        conn.close()
        print("Goodbye!")
        break
    else:
        print("Invalid choice.")

Database guarantees make the books trustworthy: a crash mid-sale cannot leave deducted-but-unrecorded stock. topics.theoryContent:
The capstone: a shopkeeper's inventory and billing system. Two tables:

products(id, name, price, stock)
sales(id, product, qty, total, day)

Features:
1. Add a product (name, price, initial stock)
2. List inventory
3. Make a sale — check stock, deduct it, record the sale, print a bill
4. Today's sales total
5. Low-stock alert (below 5)

The interesting piece is the sale: it touches TWO tables and must not do half the job. If stock is deducted but the sale row is never written (or vice versa), the books stop balancing. That is exactly what a transaction solves — and SQLite gives it to you for free.
topics.title: The full-system design

codeExamples.code:
def make_sale(cur, name, qty):
    cur.execute("SELECT id, price, stock FROM products WHERE name = ?", (name,))
    row = cur.fetchone()
    if not row:
        print("Unknown product.")
        return False
    pid, price, stock = row
    if stock < qty:
        print("Not enough stock.")
        return False
    cur.execute("UPDATE products SET stock = stock - ? WHERE id = ?", (qty, pid))
    cur.execute("INSERT INTO sales (product, qty, total, day) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)",
                (name, qty, price * qty, str(date.today())))
    return True
codeExamples.explanation: The check guards the UPDATE; caller commits once — stock and sale row land together.
codeExamples.title: Sale inside a transaction

topics.theoryContent:
A sale must be all-or-nothing. The pattern:

1. BEGIN (SQLite starts a transaction automatically on INSERT/UPDATE)
2. SELECT the current stock
3. If stock < qty → refuse, no changes
4. UPDATE products SET stock = stock - qty
5. INSERT the sales row
6. COMMIT — everything lands together

Inside a transaction, SQLite guarantees that either every statement takes effect or none do. If the program dies between steps 4 and 5, a rollback undoes the deduction — the shop never loses stock without a recorded sale. This is the database feature that makes the system trustworthy with real money.
topics.title: The atomic sale

from datetime import date

def make_sale(cur, name, qty):
    cur.execute("SELECT price, stock FROM products WHERE name = ?", (name,))
    row = cur.fetchone()
    if not row or row[1] < qty:
        print("Not enough stock or unknown product.")
        return
    price, stock = row
    cur.execute("UPDATE products SET stock = stock - ? WHERE name = ?", (qty, name))
    cur.execute("INSERT INTO sales (product, qty, total, day) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)",
                (name, qty, price * qty, str(date.today())))
    print("=" * 30)
    print(f"{name} x {qty}  = Rs {price * qty:.2f}")
    print("=" * 30)

conn = sqlite3.connect("shop.db")
cur = conn.cursor()
make_sale(cur, "Vada Pav", 3)
conn.commit()
conn.close()
codeExamples.explanation: One expression computes the bill total and the stored total, so they always match.
codeExamples.title: Bill and commit

topics.theoryContent:
After a successful sale the shopkeeper needs something to hand the customer:

def print_bill(name, qty, price):
    total = price * qty
    print("=" * 30)
    print("SHOP BILL")
    print("=" * 30)
    print(f"{name} x {qty}")
    print(f"Total: Rs {total:.2f}")
    print("Thank you, visit again!")
    print("=" * 30)

Simple f-strings with alignment give a respectable receipt. The bill is cosmetic; the important part is that total matches what was INSERTed into sales — keep the two in one calculation so they cannot diverge.
topics.title: Printing a bill

def daily_total(cur):
    cur.execute("SELECT SUM(total) FROM sales WHERE day = ?", (str(date.today()),))
    total = cur.fetchone()[0]
    print(f"Today's sales: Rs {total or 0:.2f}")

topics.theoryContent:
At ~150 lines this is the biggest program so far, and structure is what keeps it readable:

TOP: imports and constants
MIDDLE: one function per feature (add_product, list_inventory, make_sale, daily_total, low_stock)
BOTTOM: the menu loop, which only routes

Rules that keep it clean:
- No feature logic in the loop — every branch calls one function.
- Every function talks to the database through cur and conn passed in or opened inside.
- The menu is the last block, after all definitions.
- Each function is small enough to read in one screen.

The project is a proof of mastery: it uses conditionals, loops, functions, dicts/strings, exceptions, datetime, files (the .db file), and SQL. Nothing here is new — the test is putting it together without losing the plot.
topics.title: Keeping a larger program readable

commonMistakes: Revising by reading only — recall is built by writing, not by recognising.
Tackling the system problem first when it is the hardest; points are scored in order.
Leaving error handling out "because it is a test" — it is the fastest way to lose half the marks.
Building one giant main() with no functions, making bugs impossible to isolate.
Not timing the dry run, so the real exam runs long.
Stopping after the exam — the week after is when the weak days must be re-drilled.

topics.theoryContent:
Revise in four blocks. Block one, the fundamentals:

- Days 1-5: variables, types, input/conversion, operators, conditionals.
  Can you write a program that reads two numbers and prints the larger one in one sitting, no lookup?
- Days 6-10: while/for loops, strings, lists, tuples, dicts.
  Can you count word frequencies in a sentence with a dict?
- Days 11-15: functions, arguments/scope, sets, comprehensions, modules.
  Can you split a problem into three functions without being told to?

Speed matters: a master exam is timed. Every block should have ONE exercise you can produce without thinking. If you hesitate, that day goes on your practice list.

topics.theoryContent:
Block two:

- Days 16-17: exceptions and file handling. Write a read-a-file-safely function from memory.
- Days 18-20: OOP. Describe the difference between a class and an object; write a BankAccount with deposit/withdraw.
- Days 21-23: lambda, map/filter/reduce, iterators/generators. Convert a loop into a generator without reference.
- Days 24-25: regex and JSON. Validate an email and save a list of dicts to a file.

The test is not recognising the topics — it is producing code from a blank page. Recall is the skill the exam measures, and recall improves with one re-read plus one from-memory write, in that order.

topics.theoryContent:
The exam is three problems, done in ninety minutes, closed book, from a blank file. This is the pattern used across the industry for Python junior assessments:

PROBLEM 1 (20 min) — Language core
Write a program that reads student names and marks, stores them, prints the class average and the topper. (Days 1-15)

PROBLEM 2 (30 min) — Data and OOP
Design a BankAccount class with deposits, withdrawals, and a transaction log saved to a JSON file. Raise proper exceptions on insufficient funds. (Days 16-25)

PROBLEM 3 (40 min) — System
Build a small library/booking system using SQLite: add items, borrow, return, list. Keep data consistent across restarts. (Days 26-35)

Marking rewards correct structure and error handling over fancy tricks. A working simple solution scores more than a half-finished clever one.
